strategy.headline: Sell New Orleans first and the Pelicans second: paid, hand-made city craft timed to king cake, second lines and crawfish.
strategy.thesis: New Orleans fans wear the city before the team: Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl phrase tees, ward numbers and school colors beat a Pelicans logo that only dates to 2013, in a town that watched the Jazz leave and the Hornets spend two Katrina seasons in Oklahoma City. The city runs on its own clock (second-line Sundays from Labor Day to June, king cake from Jan 6 to Mardi Gras on Feb 9, 2027, crawfish from Lent through Jazz Fest), and that clock overlaps the NBA season almost exactly. After a 26-56 season, with first-year coach Jamahl Mosley and no 2026 first-round pick, standings won't sell product; craft and calendar will. Plan roughly two-thirds of units as city-first product carrying a secondary Pelicans mark and one-third as player and team product, commission the city's hands (sign painters, brass bands, bounce artists, school programs) on their terms, and drop on New Orleans dates rather than league dates.

archetype.name: The Second Line
archetype.description: They dance behind the city's main line (Saints, LSU and Carnival), loyal through two lost franchises and loud when the music is right. They buy city pride first and team gear second, and they punish anything that reads tourist.

pulse.teamMoment: New coach Jamahl Mosley inherits Zion Williamson, breakout scorer Trey Murphy III (21.5 ppg, kept through June trade rumors) and second-year Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears after a 26-56 season and a quiet offseason under Joe Dumars. The team is not on the opening-night or Christmas slates; NBA Cup West Group B (OKC, MIN, LAC, MEM), opening Oct 30 at the Clippers, is the early-season stage.
pulse.sentiment: Weary, not angry: protective of Murphy, hopeful on Queen and Fears, cautious about building anything on Zion's availability, and more excited by the 'NOLA Nights' Skelican City Edition (revived in 2025-26; 2026-27 design unverified) than by the roster.

topInsights.title: City mark first, team mark second
topInsights.insight: Locals put local phrase tees over team gear, and the Pelicans compete with Saints black-and-gold and LSU purple-and-gold for the same shirt drawer. The 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' City Edition (purple, neon green and the skeletal Skelican), brought back in 2025-26, showed that a New Orleans-after-dark story beats the standard marks.
topInsights.implication: Make every hero piece pass as New Orleans pride on the street, with the Pelicans mark as a secondary lockup, jock tag or sleeve hit, and keep a lean one-third of units team- and player-led.

topInsights.title: The NBA season is second-line season
topInsights.insight: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs parade most Sundays from Labor Day into June in new color-matched suits and fresh sneakers, the city's living fashion show, and they keep their colors secret until parade day. No other NBA market has a weekly street-style ritual on the same calendar as its home schedule.
topInsights.implication: Build tonal, color-matchable sneaker and warm-up sets for the general line, and treat any club collaboration as the club's project: paid, credited, and released only if and when the club wants.

topInsights.title: Carnival color is tourist shorthand; the city's craft isn't
topInsights.insight: Purple, green and gold is on every souvenir in the Quarter and blurs into LSU, while the team's own fan-favorite City Edition went to purple and neon green at night instead. What locals haven't seen on a jersey is the hand-made civic city: blue-and-white tile street names, sign painters' dot-bordered lettering, iron lace and brass-band drum heads.
topInsights.implication: Use commissioned craft (tile numerals, hand-lettered alphabets, iron-lace jacquard, brushed-brass hardware) as the design system, and keep Carnival color to small January accents.

topInsights.title: Food is the most precise retail clock
topInsights.insight: Pelicans attention peaks October to December, then the city's own seasons take over: king cake from Jan 6 to Feb 9, fish fries and crawfish from Ash Wednesday (Feb 10) into May, sno-balls all summer. The team already has the season's best inside joke, the King Cake Baby.
topInsights.implication: Sequence drops by what's on the table: a king cake knit on Jan 6, a crawfish-red pack from late February, nectar-cream pink for spring and summer. Never launch a hero drop in the final two weeks before Mardi Gras.

topInsights.title: Identity is ward, school and side of the river
topInsights.insight: New Orleanians place each other by high school ('What school you went to?') and by ward, which bounce records shout out by number, while the West Bank and New Orleans East rep separately. School programs like St. Aug and Edna Karr, and HBCUs like Xavier, Dillard and Southern, carry more block-level loyalty than a losing pro team.
topInsights.implication: Build modular ward and side-of-the-river product first, drawn by artists from each area, and phase school and HBCU co-brands in through each institution's own licensing office.

topInsights.title: Permanence beats promises
topInsights.insight: Basketball has left New Orleans twice, so fans in a 26-56 season worry less about wins than about whether the team is rooted here. Murphy is the player fans trust, Zion is the most famous name (and a Jordan Brand athlete), and the brown pelican itself, back from near-zero after DDT, is a comeback story nobody has put on product.
topInsights.implication: Tell 'still here' stories (pelican in her piety liners, ward and school ties) instead of contention messaging, and lead player product with whichever young players Nike actually has relationships with.

topInsights.title: The sacred line is also the market's credibility test
topInsights.insight: Black Masking Indian suits, chants and patches are sacred and individually authored, second-line regalia belongs to its clubs, and bounce was built by queer Black artists such as Katey Red and Sissy Nobby. This city beat the NFL over the 'Who Dat' letters in 2010, and it calls out brands that borrow without paying.
topInsights.implication: Pay up front and credit by name, never print or trace Indian beadwork, and get consent from each club, band and artist directly rather than through a single gatekeeper.

collection.name: Made by Hand
collection.story: New Orleans marks its identity by hand: tiles at every street corner, sign painters' lettering, sousaphone brass, king cake sugar and the crawfish table. This collection is built with the people who make those things, credited and paid, so a Pelicans fan wears the city's own handwriting instead of a souvenir.

uniform.narrative: At almost every corner in the city, the street name is set in blue-and-white tile in the sidewalk, and every New Orleanian has stood on theirs. The jersey spells NEW ORLEANS tile by tile in glazed white on a cobalt body, wraps it in an original iron-lace side panel, and puts the city's hand-made civic design on court. This is a pitch for 2027-28, since the 2026-27 set is presumably already set (design unverified); back-plan it so concept, Pelicans sign-off and NBA approval land on the league's next submission window, and run its tile and iron-lace language on 2026-27 lifestyle product in the meantime.
motifs: Square-tile block capitals set on a grid, with a tile border around the wordmark
Original iron-lace railing drawing with a hidden 'NO' monogram in the scrollwork
Pelican in her piety, the state's comeback bird, inside the collar
uniform.typography: A 'NEW ORLEANS' wordmark and numbers built square by square on a tile grid, drawn and signed by a paid New Orleans sign painter, in glazed-white fills with a thin navy outline on cobalt. No script and no fleur-de-lis in the wordmark.
details: Base: cobalt, chosen to contrast clearly with the white Association set and the navy Icon set
Waistband: ward numerals in tile type running around the band, plus WESTBANK and THE EAST
Side panel: tonal iron-lace jacquard in a deeper cobalt, with the monogram at hip height
Jock tag: debossed brass crescent-and-star roundel with the lettering artist's signature
Court: tile-bordered street-name corners at each baseline, as if the court sits on a city corner
avoid: Purple, green and gold as the lead: it is tourist shorthand, blurs into LSU, and the team's own fan-favorite purple-and-neon NOLA Nights set already owns purple
Fleur-de-lis as the hero: it reads as the Saints and as souvenir shorthand, the Pelicans mark already carries one, and its history in colonial Louisiana is a secondary reason for restraint
Black Masking Indian beadwork, plumes or chief iconography in any form, and copying any club's regalia
Katrina waterlines, FEMA X-codes, voodoo and Bourbon Street or 'N'awlins' tourist shorthand
Copying a real tiled street name, a specific building's railing, or Simon's or Dr. Bob's signature styles

partners.type: Rotating paid lineup of bounce pioneers and DJs

where: Taste: Dirty Coast on Magazine Street, Fleurty Girl's French Quarter, Metairie and Gretna doors, St. Claude pop-ups and Studio BE, where limited drops land first.
Volume: Lakeside (Metairie) and Oakwood (Gretna) mall doors and Dick's, where families buy kids jerseys and mainstream colorways.
Launch: the Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center for Ward Call, Twelfth Night and school and HBCU nights.
Regional: a Gulf South line (ward-free 'Louisiana' and 'Gulf South' tile pieces) sold in Baton Rouge, Acadiana and Gulf Coast doors and online for fans outside the metro.
when: Late October to December is peak Pelicans attention and the year's biggest gifting window.
Jan 6 to about Jan 26 for Carnival product; no hero launch in the two weeks before Mardi Gras (Feb 9).
Bayou Classic (Thanksgiving weekend), the LHSAA playoffs (February to early March) and Essence (July 4 weekend) for school-pride and visitor drops.
Late February through Jazz Fest for the lightweight stretch-run and festival palette.
how: Plan about two-thirds of units as city-first product with a secondary Pelicans mark and one-third as player and team product.
Tier the range: value kids, tee and swingman bundles for local households, and numbered keepsake pieces for visitors, with separate sell-through targets per tier.
Design for 60-80°F parade days and air-conditioned arenas: mesh, seersucker, packable shells and color-matchable tonal sets.
Pay and credit every collaborator up front and send money back visibly (instruments, school programs, corridor groups), because this market checks.

risks.risk: Cultural extraction, such as anything resembling Black Masking Indian beadwork or an unpaid second-line reference, would end Nike's credibility with the communities that set the city's style.
risks.mitigation: Keep sacred material out of every brief, pay culture bearers up front, and get written consent from each club, band and artist directly.

risks.risk: Player product depends on deals Nike may not hold: Zion is a Jordan Brand athlete with a long injury history, and Murphy, Queen and Fears' apparel arrangements are unconfirmed.
risks.mitigation: Confirm each player's arrangement before assigning product, run Zion pieces through Jordan Brand, and lead with city and ward product where deals are unclear.

risks.risk: Another sub-30-win season or a Murphy trade at the Feb 11 deadline could crater team-gear demand and feed fan worry about the team's permanence.
risks.mitigation: Hold team-branded volume to about a third, keep rapid-response tees city-only, and tell 'still here' stories rather than contention.

risks.risk: Third-party IP is everywhere: Saints fleur-de-lis treatments, 'Who Dat', krewe marks, HBCU and high school marks (some tied to other brands, and involving minors), the King Cake Baby, NBA and NBPA player rights, and Hornets-era marks owned by Charlotte.
risks.mitigation: Use original commissioned art, route school and HBCU work through each institution's licensing office, clear the King Cake Baby with the Pelicans, and keep local-brand tees free of player likenesses.

risks.risk: Unknown 2026-27 home dates could put launches on road nights, and hurricane season (June 1 to Nov 30) can wipe out summer and early-fall events; Aug 29 is a day of grief.
risks.mitigation: Pin every in-arena launch to a confirmed home date, keep digital fallbacks, and schedule nothing commercial around Aug 29.

scorecard.rationale: The starkest split in the league: New Orleans's culture is second only to New York's, but thin retail, a Saints-first city and a 26-56 team put opportunity, retail and fandom at the floor, so it is a craft market, not a volume market (brief scores: opportunity 46, culture 96, retail 34, fandom 38). Few NBA cities have a deeper or more design-ready local culture, and its calendar lines up with the season. But retail is thin (few destination sneaker doors, a modest arena store, a price-conscious core), and Pelicans fandom is small, Saints-first and weary after 26-56. The opportunity sits just below average, held up by city-first product that can sell regardless of the standings.

music.headline: In New Orleans music runs on a street calendar rather than a playlist: Sunday second lines, Carnival marching bands and bounce's ward call-outs keep the same October-to-June clock as the Pelicans, so Nike should co-sign the clubs, bands and artists who own that sound instead of sampling it.
music.summary: Jazz was born here, and the city's living sounds are just as homegrown: Tremé brass bands like Rebirth, the Sunday second lines of the Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs, the sacred chants of Black Masking Indians, and bounce, the Triggerman-driven, ward-shouting hip-hop that Big Freedia carried onto Beyoncé records. Cash Money and No Limit turned Uptown housing developments into global brands and put 'bling bling' in the dictionary. The second-line season (roughly Labor Day to June) and Carnival's marching-band season overlap the NBA season almost exactly, and Jazz Fest collides with the first round of the playoffs. Locals police hometown loyalty hard (Lil Wayne's Super Bowl LIX snub still stings), so a rebuilding Pelicans team under first-year coach Jamahl Mosley, built around Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears, should sound like the city by paying the clubs, bands and bounce artists who make it.

insights.title: Second-line Sundays run on the NBA clock
insights.detail: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as Young Men Olympian Jr. (1884), Prince of Wales and Black Men of Labor parade most Sundays from around Labor Day into June. Each club marches behind a hired brass band in a new matching suit, sash and fan scheme that stays secret until parade day, so the season tracks the Pelicans' October-to-April schedule almost exactly.
insights.implication: Build Sunday home games and drops around the second line. Commission one club per season to co-design a colorway, pay the club and its band, and underwrite the club's parade police and permit fees rather than staging a branded 'second line' for content.

insights.title: Bounce is the city's own hip-hop dialect
insights.detail: Bounce grew out of early-'90s project and block parties on the Triggerman beat (sampled from the Showboys' 'Drag Rap'), with call-and-response chants that shout out wards and housing developments, as in MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv's 1991 'Where Dey At'. Big Freedia, Katey Red and Sissy Nobby carried it through Katrina, and Freedia's voice on Beyoncé's 'Formation' and 'Break My Soul' and Drake's 'Nice for What' took it worldwide.
insights.implication: A call-and-response, ward-by-ward type system across all 17 wards is the most local typography the city offers. Launch it with bounce artists, credit the queer artists who built the genre, and drop the dated 'sissy bounce' label.

insights.title: Cash Money and No Limit made Uptown a global brand
insights.detail: Master P's No Limit (Calliope) and Birdman and Slim Williams' Cash Money (Magnolia to Hollygrove) set the late-'90s Southern rap template: Mannie Fresh's 808 production, Juvenile's 'Back That Azz Up', B.G.'s 'Bling Bling' and Lil Wayne's rise, sold through stores like Peaches Records and packaged in Pen & Pixel's chrome-and-gold covers. Juvenile's NPR Tiny Desk set with Mannie Fresh proved the catalog still lands nationally.
insights.implication: That Y2K chrome-and-diamond look lines up with the franchise's 2002 arrival in New Orleans, which makes it an honest nostalgia lane for a throwback capsule. Label marks, cover art and song titles need licensing and the artists' participation.

insights.title: Brass is the city's real arena sound
insights.detail: Tremé produced the modern brass-band explosion. Rebirth Brass Band, founded in 1983 at Joseph S. Clark High by Philip and Keith Frazier with Kermit Ruffins, still holds Tuesday nights at the Maple Leaf, and Rebirth snare drummer Derrick Tabb's The Roots of Music and the Tipitina's Foundation keep school band programs equipped. Pelicans Gold (#85714D) already reads like a tarnished sousaphone bell.
insights.implication: Make brass the material and type story: brushed-brass foil and hardware, bass-drum-head lettering, and launches led by a working brass band, each paired with an instrument donation to a school band program.

insights.title: Carnival and HBCU bands are the city's stadium sound
insights.detail: St. Augustine's Marching 100, the Seventh Ward Purple Knights who became the first Black band in the Rex parade in 1967, headline Carnival alongside Edna Karr, Warren Easton and other high-school bands. Thanksgiving weekend's Bayou Classic Battle of the Bands (Southern's Human Jukebox vs. Grambling's World Famed Tiger Marching Band) fills the Superdome next door to the Smoothie King Center.
insights.implication: Band-uniform details (frogging, epaulets, cross-belts, plumes) give a credible warm-up and shooting-shirt language for a Mardi Gras-week or Bayou Classic-weekend drop. Co-create it with a band program and pay the band back in uniforms or instruments.

insights.title: Hometown-first is the loyalty test
insights.detail: When the NFL picked Kendrick Lamar over Lil Wayne to headline Super Bowl LIX at the Superdome in February 2025, Wayne said publicly that the snub hurt, and locals took it personally even though Jon Batiste sang the anthem and Trombone Shorty played the pregame. New Orleans judges brands by whether its own artists lead.
insights.implication: Every Pelicans music collaboration should be fronted by New Orleans talent from bounce, brass or Uptown rap. A national guest can feature but never headline, and every artist's footwear and apparel deals must be cleared before outreach.

places.name: Congo Square (Louis Armstrong Park)
places.why: Enslaved and free Africans gathered here on Sundays to drum and dance in the 18th and 19th centuries; it is the root of the city's rhythm and the namesake of Jazz Fest's Congo Square stage.

places.name: Maple Leaf Bar
places.why: Rebirth Brass Band's decades-long Tuesday-night residency is the city's most dependable brass ritual.

places.name: Tipitina's
places.why: Professor Longhair's namesake room, owned by the band Galactic since 2018, and its foundation supplies instruments to school bands.

places.name: Kermit's Treme Mother-in-Law Lounge
places.why: Ernie K-Doe's mural-covered shrine, now run by trumpeter Kermit Ruffins, is a neighborhood-scale room for brass and trad jazz under the Claiborne overpass.

places.name: Preservation Hall
places.why: Since 1961 the keeper of traditional New Orleans jazz, home of the Preservation Hall Jazz Band led by Ben Jaffe.

places.name: Peaches Records
places.why: Shirani 'Peaches' Rea's shop sold early bounce and Cash Money and No Limit tapes and remains a hub for local rap and bounce.

places.name: Louisiana Music Factory
places.why: The deepest stock of local music in the city, with in-store sets during festival season.

places.name: WWOZ 90.7 FM
places.why: The listener-supported jazz and heritage station posts the weekly second-line schedule, broadcasts Jazz Fest, and carries tastemaker shows such as DJ Soul Sister's.

places.name: Dew Drop Inn
places.why: The Chitlin' Circuit hub where Little Richard, Allen Toussaint and Irma Thomas played reopened as a hotel and music lounge in 2023.

places.name: Q93 (WQUE 93.3 FM)
places.why: The city's hip-hop station breaks local rap and bounce records and is the mainstream outlet for any Pelicans-linked music drop.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: The genre's global face through Beyoncé's 'Formation' and 'Break My Soul' and Drake's 'Nice for What', and the natural lead for any bounce-rooted Pelicans activation.

people.name: Juvenile
people.why: 'Back That Azz Up', produced by Mannie Fresh, is the city's party anthem, and his NPR Tiny Desk set with Mannie Fresh renewed his national reach.

people.name: Lil Wayne
people.why: The city's biggest rap star, whose Super Bowl LIX snub made him a symbol of hometown loyalty.

people.name: Trombone Shorty (Troy Andrews)
people.why: He has become a regular Jazz Fest closer, hosts the Treme Threauxdown, and runs a foundation and academy for young musicians, which makes him a credible youth-music partner.

people.name: Rebirth Brass Band
people.why: The band that modernized brass with funk and hip-hop and the standard every second-line band is measured against.

people.name: Jon Batiste
people.why: A Grammy Album of the Year winner who sang the anthem at Super Bowl LIX in the Superdome; he bridges the city's jazz lineage and mainstream pop.

people.name: Tank and the Bangas
people.role: Soul, funk and spoken-word band led by Tarriona 'Tank' Ball
people.why: Winners of NPR's 2017 Tiny Desk Contest and 2020 Best New Artist Grammy nominees, with a playful, colorful visual identity suited to co-designed product.

people.name: Rob49
people.why: The rising street-rap name of the 2020s through his 'Vulture Island' mixtapes and street-rap hits like 'On Dat Money', and the artist younger fans now rep.

moments.name: Second-line season
moments.timing: Most Sundays, from around Labor Day into June
moments.why: Social Aid & Pleasure Club parades with brass bands run through the entire NBA season and give the city a weekly street ritual to align Sunday home games and drops with.

moments.name: Bayou Classic Battle of the Bands
moments.why: Southern's Human Jukebox and Grambling's Tiger Marching Band face off next door to the Smoothie King Center; it is the biggest HBCU band moment of the year.

moments.name: Mardi Gras (Carnival parade season)
moments.timing: Late January through Fat Tuesday, Feb. 9, 2027
moments.why: High-school marching bands like St. Augustine's Marching 100 are the parades' real headliners, and the whole city is outside in purple, green and gold.

moments.name: Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night
moments.why: Black Masking Indian tribes come out in new hand-sewn suits with chants and drums; it is a sacred community event to respect, not a brand stage.

moments.name: French Quarter Festival
moments.why: A free, locals-heavy festival of hometown acts that lands as the regular season ends.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds Race Course
moments.why: The city's biggest music event overlaps the first round of the playoffs and pulls the national music press to town.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: The country's largest Black music and culture festival keeps New Orleans in the national conversation during the offseason and Summer League.

moments.name: Satchmo SummerFest
moments.timing: Early August, around Louis Armstrong's Aug. 4 birthday
moments.why: A hometown tribute to Armstrong at the Old U.S. Mint that bridges the offseason to second-line season.

vocabulary.meaning: The crowd that follows a club and its brass band (the 'main line') through the streets; also the Sunday parade itself and the dance.
The high-energy, improvised footwork of the second line; also the root of the Lady and Men Buckjumpers club name.
Bounce's signature call-and-response, answered by shouting your ward or neighborhood; from MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv's 1991 record.
The looped drum break, from the Showboys' 'Drag Rap', that sits under nearly every bounce record.
One of the city's 17 political districts; 'What ward you from?' is a core identity question and the backbone of bounce shout-outs (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, 17th Ward).
Close friend or partner, popularized nationally by Cash Money-era New Orleans rap.
Flashy jewelry and shine; coined on B.G.'s 1999 Cash Money single and later added to the Oxford English Dictionary.
The sacred hymn that opens and closes Black Masking Indian gatherings; recognize it, never use it in marketing.

designCues.cue: Pelicans Gold treated as sousaphone brass: brushed-brass foil, metal aglets and zipper pulls in Pelicans Gold against Pelicans Navy (#0C2340).
designCues.source: The worn horns of Tremé brass bands, especially the sousaphone bell that leads every second line.
designCues.use: Foil, embroidery thread and hardware on a brass-themed capsule, with the story tied to a named working band rather than generic 'jazz'.

designCues.cue: Bass-drum-head lettering: band name arched across the top of a circle and city or year across the bottom, in sign-painter script with outlines and drop shadows.
designCues.source: The hand-painted bass drum heads carried by Rebirth, TBC and other brass bands on the street.
designCues.use: A circular 'drum head' lockup for chest graphics, patches and hangtags; commission a New Orleans sign painter and never copy an existing band's drum.

designCues.cue: Parade-day regalia: satin, sequins, rhinestones, ostrich-plume fans, streamers and decorated umbrellas in a club's coordinated colors.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Club sashes, fans and umbrellas made by members for each year's parade.
designCues.use: Satin taping, sequin patches and a printed second-line handkerchief on a limited Sunday capsule, commissioned from the club members who make the regalia.

designCues.cue: The annual color reveal: each club keeps its new suit colors secret until it steps out of the hall on parade day.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Club parade tradition.
designCues.use: Run a capsule or City Edition launch as a parade-day reveal with a partner club instead of a leak-then-drop rollout.

designCues.cue: Call-and-response type: stacked shout-outs ('WHERE DEY AT?' / 'SEVENTH WARD!') in tall condensed caps, one ward per line.
designCues.source: Bounce chants that call out wards and neighborhoods.
designCues.use: Ward-by-ward tees and shooting shirts co-written with bounce artists; use ward numbers rather than demolished housing-project names unless artists from those communities lead.

designCues.cue: Y2K chrome: beveled chrome and gold 3D type, diamonds, flames and stacked photo collage.
designCues.source: Pen & Pixel Graphics' late-'90s album covers for No Limit and Cash Money.
designCues.use: Reference for a 2002-era throwback capsule; commission original art and license any label marks or cover references.

designCues.cue: Marching-band silhouette: frogging, epaulets, cross-belts and plumed-shako proportions.
designCues.source: St. Augustine's Marching 100 and the high-school and HBCU bands of Carnival and the Bayou Classic.
designCues.use: A warm-up jacket and shooting shirt with braid and frogging trim for Mardi Gras week or Bayou Classic weekend, co-created with a band program.

designCues.cue: Carnival purple, the shade locals wait for on the parade route when the Purple Knights' band comes into view.
designCues.source: Rex's 1872 purple, green and gold, and St. Augustine's purple-and-gold Marching 100.
designCues.use: Accent with Pelicans Navy and Gold on a Mardi Gras-week drop; skip literal beads, masks and jester clichés.

productHooks: 'Second Line Sunday' capsule: a satin-trimmed warm-up, printed handkerchief and drum-head tee in a colorway co-designed with one Social Aid & Pleasure Club, revealed parade-style before a Sunday home game, with proceeds covering the club's parade fees.
'Where Dey At' ward pack: 17 ward tees and a shooting shirt in bounce call-and-response type, launched by Big Freedia or another bounce artist with an in-arena bounce set.

Brass series: Pelicans Gold foil-and-hardware hoodies and tees, each drop credited to a named brass band (Rebirth first) and paired with an instrument donation through the Tipitina's Foundation or The Roots of Music.

Marching-band warm-up for Mardi Gras week and Bayou Classic weekend: a frogging-trimmed jacket in Carnival purple, Pelicans Navy and Gold, co-created with St. Augustine's Marching 100 or another band program.
Jazz Fest-window playoff tee: a commissioned poster-style print by a Black New Orleans artist, dropped when the festival overlaps the first round, with no Jazz Fest marks used without a license.
watchouts: Black Masking (Mardi Gras) Indian suits, beaded patches, chants such as 'Indian Red' and Big Chiefs' names are sacred and individually authored: never reproduce or sample them, and only commission, credit and pay masking artists who choose to take part.
Bounce was built by queer artists (Big Freedia, Katey Red, Sissy Nobby): credit and pay them, don't use the culture as edgy flavor, and avoid the dated 'sissy bounce' tag.
Songs ('Back That Azz Up', 'Iko Iko'), label marks (Cash Money, No Limit), Pen & Pixel art and the Jazz Fest, Tipitina's and Preservation Hall names are third-party IP that need licensing.

Second lines are working-class Black neighborhood institutions under pressure from gentrification, permit costs and past violence on parade routes: no staged branded second lines, no parade photography without the clubs' consent, and fair pay for bands.

Housing-project names (Magnolia, Calliope, Lafitte, St. Bernard, Desire) recall public housing demolished after Katrina and residents displaced; use them only when artists from those communities lead, and clear each artist's footwear and apparel contracts before outreach.

art.headline: New Orleans looks made by hand — tile-set street names, glitter-dotted sign painting, iron lace, gilded floats and hand-sewn Black Masking Indian beadwork — and with the 2023-24 'Skelican' City Edition already having claimed purple and neon green, Nike's next move is commissioning those hands.
art.summary: The city's look is architectural and handmade: the Pontalba Buildings' 'AP' monogram cast into iron lace, blue-and-white tile street names set into sidewalk corners, crescent-and-star water meter covers, olive-green St. Charles streetcars and the hand-painted signs of Simon of New Orleans and Dr. Bob. Its street art is a story of reclamation, from Brandan 'BMike' Odums painting abandoned housing developments before opening Studio BE in a Bywater warehouse, to Tremé painting live oaks back onto the I-10 columns that replaced Claiborne Avenue's neutral ground. Carnival runs two visual systems at once: the old-line krewes' gilded papier-mâché floats, flambeaux and Rex's purple, green and gold, and the Black street Carnival of Indian beadwork, Baby Doll satin and Social Aid & Pleasure Club suits and umbrellas, which belongs to its makers. The 2023-24 fan-favorite City Edition, brought back in 2025-26, showed locals reward city color over team color; the next step is commissioned craft (sign-painter lettering, tile numerals, iron-lace patterning, paid Black New Orleans artists), not more fleur-de-lis.

insights.title: Carnival is two visual systems, not one
insights.detail: Old-line krewes speak in gilded papier-mâché floats, flambeaux and aluminum doubloons (introduced by Rex in 1960), under the purple, green and gold Rex chose in 1872. Black street Carnival speaks in Black Masking Indian beadwork, Baby Doll satin bonnets and the North Side Skull and Bone Gang's papier-mâché skulls at dawn in Tremé.
insights.implication: The krewe palette is already on the fan-favorite City Edition, so repeating it adds little; the untapped layer is craft, and the Black street-Carnival layer can only enter product through named, paid collaborators, never as surface pattern.

insights.title: The defining walls are under the interstate and inside abandoned buildings
insights.detail: The I-10 overpass built over Claiborne Avenue in the late 1960s erased the oak-lined neutral ground at the heart of Black Tremé; its columns are now painted with oaks, Indians and neighborhood history, and Indians and families gather there on Mardi Gras Day. BMike Odums built his name painting the abandoned Florida housing development (the Project Be and Exhibit Be shows) and Algiers' DeGaulle Manor before opening Studio BE in Bywater.
insights.implication: New Orleans street art means painting back what was lost after Katrina and urban renewal; commission Tremé, Seventh Ward and Ninth Ward artists for new work in that spirit instead of reproducing existing murals.

insights.title: The city's lettering is hand-painted and tile-set
insights.detail: Street names are spelled in blue-and-white tile at sidewalk corners, Simon of New Orleans' dot-bordered, glittered signs hang in bars and restaurants citywide, Dr. Bob's 'Be Nice or Leave' signs are painted on found wood framed in bottle caps, and sno-ball stands and corner stores still hand-letter their menus.
insights.implication: Generic sports script reads as anywhere; a commissioned hand-lettered alphabet and tile-set numerals would read as New Orleans at a glance, on jerseys, warm-ups and retail graphics.

insights.title: The fleur-de-lis is a trap, and the city defends its symbols
insights.detail: The fleur-de-lis reads as the Saints, and Louisiana's 1724 Code Noir ordered recaptured runaway enslaved people branded with it. In 2010, when the NFL sent cease-and-desist letters to local shops such as Fleurty Girl over 'Who Dat' shirts, the backlash from fans and state officials made the league back off.
insights.implication: Lead with other cues, never try to claim a local phrase as Nike or NBA property, and treat local tee makers as partners rather than infringers.

insights.title: Status is earned by hand
insights.detail: Big Chiefs spend most of a year sewing suits from tens of thousands of beads, rhinestones and plumes, competing to be the 'prettiest', and Demond Melancon's beadwork now hangs in museums and galleries; Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs debut new coordinated suits, sashes and decorated umbrellas each parade, and Krewe of Red Beans members glue bean mosaics onto suits.
insights.implication: Hand-finished, numbered, artist-signed pieces carry more local prestige than any print; build the top tier of a New Orleans collection around makers' handwork, with the makers paid and credited.

insights.title: A Carnival fabrication bench works year-round
insights.detail: Kern Studios, whose Mardi Gras World warehouses sit on the riverfront, and independent float builders sculpt foam, papier-mâché and gold leaf all year; when COVID canceled the 2021 parades, Devin De Wulf's Hire a Mardi Gras Artist paid out-of-work float artists to turn homes into 'house floats'.
insights.implication: Commission float artists for Smoothie King Center installations, retail fixtures and a Carnival-season pop-up, so the activation is built by the same hands that build the parades.

places.name: Studio BE
places.why: BMike Odums's warehouse of monumental spray-painted portraits and text pieces is the city's best-known contemporary street-art space and the clearest route to a credible collaborator.

places.name: Claiborne Avenue overpass columns ('under the bridge')
places.neighborhood: Tremé / Seventh Ward (N. Claiborne Ave under I-10)
places.why: Columns painted with live oaks and Black New Orleans history stand where the neutral ground was lost, and on Mardi Gras Day they frame the city's most important street gathering.

places.name: St. Claude Arts District
places.neighborhood: Marigny / St. Roch / Bywater (St. Claude Ave)
places.why: Artist-run spaces such as The Front and Good Children Gallery hold Second Saturday openings, making it the scene's experimental, emerging-artist end.

places.name: Julia Street Arts District
places.why: Established galleries such as Arthur Roger Gallery and Jonathan Ferrara Gallery represent the city's major painters and host White Linen Night and Art for Art's Sake.

places.name: Ogden Museum of Southern Art
places.neighborhood: Warehouse District (Camp St at Lee Circle)
places.why: The deepest collection of Southern art and self-taught work, with Thursday-night Ogden After Hours concerts that draw a local creative crowd.

places.name: Ashé Cultural Arts Center
places.why: Founded by Carol Bebelle and Douglas Redd, it anchors Black visual art, Indian and second-line culture on the boulevard and is a natural co-host for community-led product.

places.name: Mardi Gras World (Kern Studios)
places.neighborhood: Riverfront by the Convention Center (Port of New Orleans Place)
places.why: The warehouses where Carnival floats are sculpted, painted and gilded hold the city's largest commercial fabrication talent pool.

places.name: Music Box Village
places.neighborhood: Bywater (N. Rampart St near the Industrial Canal)
places.why: New Orleans Airlift's playable houses built from salvage show the city's make-it-from-what's-left design ethic and host concerts and fabrication.

places.name: The Historic New Orleans Collection
places.neighborhood: French Quarter (Royal St and Chartres St)
places.why: The best archive of the city's maps, Carnival design drawings, signage and ironwork — where designers should research before drawing anything.

places.name: Xavier University of Louisiana, Department of Art
places.why: MacArthur Fellow sculptor John T. Scott taught here for four decades, and it remains a pipeline for Black New Orleans artists and designers.

people.name: Brandan 'BMike' Odums
people.role: Painter, muralist and filmmaker; founder of Studio BE
people.why: His large spray-painted portraits of civil-rights and local figures, born in Project Be and Exhibit Be, make him the most credible New Orleans street artist for a City Edition or Black history collaboration.

people.name: Demond Melancon
people.role: Big Chief of the Young Seminole Hunters; beadwork artist
people.why: His hand-beaded suits and portrait panels cross from the street to museums, the model for a paid, credited, maker-led beadwork commission.

people.name: Willie Birch
people.role: Painter and sculptor of Seventh Ward life
people.why: His large black-and-white drawings of second lines, porches and neighbors are the elder-statesman record of the Seventh Ward, so a tribute or commission would carry real weight there.

people.name: Bruce Davenport Jr.
people.role: Lower Ninth Ward artist known for marker drawings of marching bands
people.why: His dense, colorful drawings of high-school marching bands bridge New Orleans' band culture and sports spectacle, a natural fit for game-night and youth product.

people.name: Simon of New Orleans (Simon Hardeveld)
people.why: His bright, dot-bordered, glittered signs signed 'Simon' hang all over the city and define its hand-lettered look.

people.name: Dr. Bob (Bob Shaffer)
people.why: His 'Be Nice or Leave' signs on salvaged wood framed in bottle caps are the city's most-recognized hand-painted phrase.

people.name: L. Kasimu Harris
people.why: His series on vanishing Black bars and lounges documents Black New Orleans social life from inside, making him a credible lens for campaign and product storytelling.

people.name: Fleurty Girl (Lauren Haydel)
people.why: A target of the NFL's 2010 'Who Dat' cease-and-desist letters, it is the local face of the city's own fan-tee vernacular and a natural rapid-response partner.

moments.name: Twelfth Night opens Carnival
moments.timing: January 6 (Joan of Arc parade in the French Quarter; Phunny Phorty Phellows ride the St. Charles streetcar)
moments.why: The city switches into Carnival look and color for six weeks, the natural launch for a Carnival-season drop.

moments.name: Lundi Gras and Mardi Gras Day
moments.why: Krewe of Red Beans bean suits on Lundi Gras, then Zulu, Rex, Indians, Baby Dolls and the Skull and Bone Gang on the day — the year's peak of street costume and craft.

moments.name: Uptown Super Sunday
moments.timing: Sunday near St. Joseph's Day (March 19), traditionally from A.L. Davis Park in Central City
moments.why: Black Masking Indian tribes show their suits in daylight, the moment to meet chiefs about commissions, as guests, never as a marketing backdrop.

moments.name: Jazz Fest and its posters
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May
moments.why: The official Jazz Fest and Congo Square silkscreen posters are a decades-old collector tradition that proves New Orleanians buy numbered local art prints.

moments.name: White Linen Night
moments.timing: First Saturday of August, Julia Street
moments.why: The Warehouse District's summer gallery night is an offseason stage for an artist reveal before the season starts.

moments.name: Art for Art's Sake
moments.timing: First Saturday of October, Julia Street and Magazine Street
moments.why: The gallery season opener lands weeks before tip-off, a ready-made unveiling for City Edition art or an artist-in-residence.

moments.name: Second-line Sundays
moments.timing: Most Sundays, roughly late August through June
moments.why: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs parade in new coordinated suits, sashes and umbrellas each year; this is the city's living fashion show.

moments.name: Monthly gallery nights
moments.timing: Second Saturday on St. Claude Ave; first Saturday on Julia St

vocabulary.meaning: A covered porch or upper porch held up by posts from the street; locals and preservationists distinguish it from a cantilevered balcony.
The ornamental cast and wrought iron on French Quarter and Garden District galleries and fences, such as the Pontalba 'AP' railings and the Cornstalk fence on Royal St.
A Carnival organization that parades or holds a ball; now used for any crew with a shared purpose.
What riders toss from floats: beads, cups, doubloons and coveted hand-decorated pieces such as Zulu coconuts and Muses shoes.
Making and wearing a costume; to 'mask Indian' means sewing and wearing a suit as a Black Masking Indian, a year-long commitment.
The crowd that dances behind a club and its brass band (the 'main line') in a Sunday parade or jazz funeral.
The median of a boulevard, where families stake out parade spots and where Claiborne's lost oaks once stood.
A little something extra given for free, a natural name for a hidden inside-the-collar or jock-tag detail.

designCues.cue: Sidewalk-tile cobalt (approx. #1E4D9B) on glazed white (approx. #F3F0E6), set as square-tile block capitals with a tile border.
designCues.source: The tiled street names inlaid at sidewalk corners across the French Quarter, Marigny and Uptown.
designCues.use: Numbers, neighborhood names (TREMÉ, ST. CLAUDE, CENTRAL CITY) and a 'NEW ORLEANS' wordmark built tile by tile, a typographic system no other city has.

designCues.cue: St. Charles streetcar green, a dark olive (approx. #3F5B37; match to the RTA paint), trimmed with gold numerals.
designCues.source: The 1923-24 Perley Thomas cars still running on the St. Charles line, the world's oldest continuously operating street railway.
designCues.use: A fall lifestyle base or alternate colorway with Pelicans gold numerals; the roller-sign destination type can inspire secondary lettering.

designCues.cue: Iron lace: repeating cast-iron gallery railing with a monogram hidden in the scrollwork.
designCues.source: The Pontalba Buildings' railings on Jackson Square, with the Baroness de Pontalba's 'AP' cast in, and French Quarter galleries and fences.
designCues.use: Laser-cut perforations, jacquard knits and shorts side panels with a 'NO' or Pelicans monogram woven into an original railing drawing, not a copy of a specific building.

designCues.cue: Hand-painted sign lettering: bright caps outlined in dots, glitter fills and found-wood borders.
designCues.source: Simon of New Orleans' glittered signs, Dr. Bob's bottle-cap-framed 'Be Nice or Leave' and hand-lettered sno-ball stand menus.
designCues.use: Commission a New Orleans sign painter to hand-letter an original 'PELICANS' / 'NEW ORLEANS' alphabet for lifestyle graphics, signed and credited; never imitate Simon's or Dr. Bob's signature style without them.

designCues.cue: Crescent moon and stars inside a cast-iron circle.
designCues.source: The city's cast-iron water meter covers, whose crescent-and-star motif nods to the 'Crescent City' nickname and is already a beloved rubbing and print subject.
designCues.use: A debossed jock tag, outsole or patch icon; a quiet 'Crescent City' mark for locals that avoids the fleur-de-lis.

designCues.cue: The doubloon: a coin with the krewe emblem on one face and the year's theme on the other, struck in anodized aluminum (purple, green and gold among many colors).
designCues.source: Doubloons, introduced by Rex in 1960, are the throw every Carnival kid scrambles for.
designCues.use: Two-sided metal jock tags, hang tags and limited Pelicans doubloons with a new theme each season, made with or licensed from a doubloon maker and never copying a krewe's emblem.

designCues.cue: Second-line regalia: satin sashes, ribbon fringe, sequins and feather-trimmed umbrellas in each club's color of the year.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as Black Men of Labor, Lady Buckjumpers and Prince of Wales, which reveal new outfits on parade day.
designCues.use: Satin and fringe trims for a fan-wear capsule made with a named club, which picks the colors, gets paid and is credited; no generic 'second-line' costume.

designCues.cue: 'Pretty': the Black Masking Indian ethic of a year of handwork, bead by bead, worn once in the street.
designCues.source: Big Chiefs such as Demond Melancon, and the Uptown and Downtown beadwork traditions.
designCues.use: A story of craft and refusal to bow down, told through one-of-one pieces a Big Chief makes on their own terms; never print, scan or trace a suit or its patches.

productHooks: 'Claiborne Oaks' Black history capsule: commission Tremé and Seventh Ward artists (BMike Odums, or artists in the Willie Birch lineage) to paint the lost live oaks back, rendered as wraparound side panels and a numbered print, with proceeds to a Claiborne Corridor community group the artists choose.

'Throws' Carnival drop from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027): two-sided Pelicans doubloon jock tags, tile-letter neighborhood tees and a float-artist-built pop-up at Smoothie King Center.
Sign-painter wordmark line: a commissioned hand-lettered New Orleans alphabet with dot-border trims and glitter ink, launched at Art for Art's Sake or a Second Saturday on St. Claude.
'Streetcar' colorway: dark olive green with gold numerals and iron-lace laser-cut panels for a fall shooting shirt, warm-up and lifestyle jacket.

One-of-one beaded patch by a Big Chief such as Demond Melancon for a framed jersey or charity auction, with full fee, credit and the chief's control of the design; no printed beadwork on mass product.
Pre-cleared rapid-response tees with local makers like Fleurty Girl for big Zion or Trey Murphy III moments, so the city's own tee vernacular becomes official product.
watchouts: Black Masking Indian suits, patches and roles are spiritual and ancestral, and each belongs to its maker; never print, scan or trace them, avoid headdress or 'chief' iconography, keep them separate from Native American imagery generally, and work only through named Big Chiefs and Big Queens, paid and credited.

Lead with something other than the fleur-de-lis: it reads as the Saints, and the 1724 Code Noir used it to brand enslaved people. After the 2010 'Who Dat' fight, any attempt to claim a local phrase or symbol will backfire.

Murals (Studio BE, the Claiborne columns), krewe names and emblems (Rex, Zulu coconuts, Muses shoes), Jazz Fest marks and posters, Dr. Bob's 'Be Nice or Leave' and Simon's signature style are owned; license or commission, never lift.
Do not decorate with Katrina: FEMA search 'X-codes', water lines and flood imagery are trauma markers, and Lower Ninth Ward or Seventh Ward stories need local co-authors.

Bywater and St. Claude are gentrification flashpoints, and second lines are community property: hire clubs, brass bands and Black New Orleans artists from the Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward and Central City rather than staging a second line for marketing.

verify: Studio BE (2941 Royal St, Bywater) is still open and Brandan 'BMike' Odums takes commissions.
What the 2026-27 City Edition will be (the 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' Skelican design returned in 2025-26).
Carnival 2027 dates (Twelfth Night Jan 6; Krewe of Red Beans on Lundi Gras Feb 8; Mardi Gras Day Feb 9) and the Pelicans' home games around them.
Uptown Super Sunday 2027 date and its start at A.L. Davis Park.
The Claiborne overpass column murals are intact, and the status of any I-10 Claiborne Expressway removal or redevelopment plan.
Simon of New Orleans (Simon Hardeveld) and Dr. Bob (Bob Shaffer) are still painting and selling from their studios.
Demond Melancon still leads the Young Seminole Hunters and accepts commissions.
The Front and Good Children Gallery are operating on St. Claude and Second Saturday openings continue.
Arthur Roger Gallery and Jonathan Ferrara Gallery are open on Julia St, and Willie Birch is still represented by Arthur Roger.
White Linen Night (first Saturday of August) and Art for Art's Sake (first Saturday of October) are still held.

Prospect.7 dates, a possible citywide art stage during the 2027-28 season.

food.headline: New Orleans eats by the calendar (king cake, then crawfish, then sno-balls), and its proudest kitchens are Black Creole and Vietnamese, which makes food the most precise seasonal clock Nike has for Pelicans city product.
food.summary: New Orleans keeps time by what is in season: king cake from Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras, crawfish through Lent and Jazz Fest, sno-balls all summer, gumbo when the weather turns. The institutions that carry it are Black Creole (Dooky Chase's, Willie Mae's), neighborhood (Parkway, Leidenheimer, Hansen's) and Vietnamese (Dong Phuong in New Orleans East), and the street food of second-line Sundays (yakamein, huckabucks) runs on the same October-to-June clock as the NBA. The Pelicans already own one great food joke, the King Cake Baby, and play in an arena named for a smoothie chain born in metro New Orleans. Coming off 26-56, with first-year coach Jamahl Mosley and low expectations, city-pride product will carry this season more than roster product, and food is the sharpest way to time it. Every food collab needs paid local partners and food-brand licensing.

insights.title: Carnival is the Pelicans' food season
insights.detail: King cake season runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027), right through the heart of the home schedule, and locals argue over cakes from Dong Phuong, Haydel's and Manny Randazzo. The Pelicans already own the food's best inside joke: the unnerving King Cake Baby mascot that has haunted Carnival-season games since 2015.
insights.implication: Build the season's biggest city-specific drop around king cake rather than generic beads: release it on Jan 6, use the team-owned King Cake Baby, and pay a local bakery to make the co-branded box.

insights.title: Tremé's Black Creole kitchens are civic institutions
insights.detail: Leah Chase's Dooky Chase's fed Freedom Riders and civil rights organizers and still serves gumbo z'herbes on Holy Thursday (Mar 25, 2027). Willie Mae's Scotch House, a few blocks away, is the city's fried-chicken benchmark. Both sit in the Tremé and Seventh Ward corridor that the I-10 Claiborne overpass cut through in the 1960s.
insights.implication: The deepest food story in this market is Black Creole and family-owned, so tell it only through paid partnerships with these families and send proceeds back to the Claiborne corridor.

insights.title: The po-boy is a labor story on Central City bread
insights.detail: Locals trace the name to the 1929 streetcar strike, when ex-conductors Bennie and Clovis Martin fed striking 'poor boys' for free, and the loaf has come from Leidenheimer on Simon Bolivar Avenue in Central City since 1896. Ordering is coded: 'dressed' means lettuce, tomato, pickle and mayo, and 'debris' is the roast-beef gravy at Parkway.
insights.implication: A working-class origin story fits a team in a lean year. Use the butcher-paper wrap, the order ticket and the strike story for packaging and naming, and time it to the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

insights.title: Vietnamese New Orleans makes Tết a home-market moment
insights.detail: Refugees who arrived after 1975 built Village de l'Est in New Orleans East around Mary Queen of Vietnam church, whose Tết festival falls near Lunar New Year (Feb 6, 2027), inside Carnival. Dong Phuong's loaves carry the city's banh mi ('Vietnamese po-boys') and its king cake sells out every year, while the West Bank (Gretna, Harvey) has its own pho-and-grocery corridor.
insights.implication: A Lunar New Year piece here is local, not borrowed from a coastal playbook: co-design it with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and Dong Phuong instead of using generic zodiac graphics.

insights.title: Second-line Sundays come with their own menu
insights.detail: From late summer to spring, Social Aid and Pleasure Club parades through Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City are trailed by yakamein ('Old Sober') vendors, led in public by Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady, while front porches sell huckabucks (frozen Kool-Aid cups). The season lines up almost exactly with the NBA's.
insights.implication: This is Black neighborhood culture, not set dressing: engage through Feed the Second Line and paid collabs with vendors and clubs, and never print club names or regalia without permission.

insights.title: The arena and the beer are already food brands
insights.detail: Fans watch games in an arena named for Smoothie King, founded in metro New Orleans in 1973, and owner Gayle Benson owns Faubourg Brewing (formerly Dixie Beer), renamed from Dixie Beer in 2020 over the name's Confederate associations. Pelicans game day is a quick downtown pre-game crowd; the big tailgate culture belongs to the Saints next door.
insights.implication: Food collabs must clear the team's naming and beverage partners first, and activation should sit in the arena and along the Poydras corridor rather than in a parking-lot tailgate.

insights.title: Crawfish and sno-balls bookend the stretch run
insights.detail: Crawfish boils peak from March to May, through Lenten fish fries and Jazz Fest (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys). Sno-ball stands like Hansen's Sno-Bliz (since 1939) reopen in spring with nectar cream, a pink vanilla-almond flavor found almost nowhere else.
insights.implication: Give the late season and any play-in run its own palette, boiled-crawfish red and nectar pink, instead of reusing Carnival purple, green and gold.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: Leah Chase's Creole dining room, where civil rights strategy was planned over gumbo, is the most respected food address in Black New Orleans.

places.name: Willie Mae's Scotch House
places.why: Its fried chicken was named a James Beard America's Classic in 2005, and volunteers rebuilt it after Katrina, so it stands for neighborhood recovery.

places.name: Parkway Bakery & Tavern
places.why: Since 1911 it has been the roast beef debris and fried shrimp po-boy that locals take visitors to, and its T-shirts are worn around town.

places.name: Leidenheimer Baking Company
places.why: It has baked the thin-crust French bread under most of the city's po-boys since 1896.

places.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
places.why: Its banh mi loaves and butter-and-cream-cheese king cake draw lines from every corner of the metro.

places.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
places.why: This family stand, open since 1939, is the reference point for shaved-ice sno-balls and house-made syrups like nectar cream.

places.name: Café Reconcile
places.why: It trains young New Orleanians for hospitality jobs over red beans and fried catfish on the Oretha Castle Haley corridor, which makes it a natural community partner.

places.name: Hong Kong Food Market
places.why: It anchors Vietnamese and pan-Asian grocery shopping on the West Bank, the other half of the city's Vietnamese food map.

places.name: Turkey and the Wolf
places.why: Mason Hereford's sandwich shop has hand-scrawled, irreverent merch that young locals wear as a style signal.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The home court is named for a smoothie chain founded in metro New Orleans, and its concession and beverage partners set the limits for any in-arena food collab.

people.name: Dooky Chase's (the Chase family)
people.role: Tremé restaurant family of Leah Chase (1923-2019), the 'Queen of Creole Cuisine'
people.why: Leah's grandson, chef Edgar 'Dook' Chase IV, and the family keep up the Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes and a dining room hung with African American art, so any Creole-pride product should start with their consent.

people.name: Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady
people.why: Her yakamein at second lines and Jazz Fest, along with national TV appearances, made 'Old Sober' a citywide symbol of Black New Orleans street food.

people.name: Nina Compton
people.role: Saint Lucian-born chef of Compère Lapin; 2018 James Beard Best Chef: South
people.why: She was a finalist on Top Chef's New Orleans season and became the city's leading Caribbean-Creole voice, linking New Orleans to the wider Black Atlantic table.

people.name: Serigne Mbaye
people.why: His tasting menu cooks the West African roots of Creole food (okra, rice, and gumbo's own name), a high-end voice for the diaspora story.

people.name: Mason Hereford
people.role: Chef-owner of Turkey and the Wolf and Molly's Rise and Shine
people.why: His thrift-store, hand-drawn design language and Bon Appétit's 2017 Best New Restaurant title turned a sandwich shop into a style reference for young locals.

people.name: Hubig's Pies
people.why: Its Savory Simon mascot became a cult T-shirt in the decade the pies were gone after the 2012 bakery fire, before they returned in 2022, proof that locals wear food brands as loyalty.

people.name: Krewe of Red Beans / Feed the Second Line
people.role: Lundi Gras bean-mosaic parade krewe and the culture-bearer nonprofit it started (founder Devin De Wulf)
people.why: The krewe turns a Monday dish into costume art and the nonprofit sends money to Black Masking Indians, second-line club members and musicians, which makes them a credible partner for red-beans product.

people.name: Poppy Tooker
people.role: Host of WWNO's 'Louisiana Eats!' and food historian
people.why: As the city's best-known food explainer, she is the right person to check a food story before it goes on product.

moments.name: King cake season (Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras)
moments.why: It runs through prime home dates, king cakes fill every office, and the King Cake Baby comes out at Pelicans games.

moments.name: Tết at Mary Queen of Vietnam
moments.why: New Orleans East's biggest community gathering, full of food stalls, lands inside Carnival.

moments.name: Red Beans Parade (Krewe of Red Beans)
moments.why: Bean-mosaic costumes parade through the downtown neighborhoods, turning Monday's dish into wearable art.

moments.name: Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes at Dooky Chase's
moments.why: Leah Chase's Lenten green gumbo is the year's most coveted lunch, a late-season story moment.

moments.name: Crawfish season and Lenten Friday fish fries
moments.timing: Peaks March to May; Lenten Fridays Feb 12 - Mar 26, 2027
moments.why: Backyard boils and church fish fries are where fans gather during the stretch run.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds
moments.why: Its food booths (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys, Ms. Linda's yakamein) are a city ritual that collides with play-in and playoff dates.

moments.name: Treme Creole Gumbo Festival
moments.why: This free festival pairs gumbo with brass bands in Tremé during the first month of the season.

moments.name: Oak Street Po-Boy Festival
moments.why: A street festival for the city's sandwich and a natural launch for po-boy product.

vocabulary.meaning: A po-boy with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayo; 'shrimp, dressed' is a complete order.
The gravy-soaked roast-beef shreds from the pan, ordered on a po-boy (said DAY-bree).
A little something extra thrown in for free (said LAN-yap); used for any bonus.
Louis Armstrong's letter sign-off, a nod to the Monday red beans tradition that grew out of wash day.
A frozen Kool-Aid cup sold from a neighbor's front door; also called a frozen cup or cold cup.
Yakamein, the beef-noodle soup with egg and green onion sold at second lines as a hangover cure.
The pink vanilla-almond sno-ball flavor topped with condensed milk; it's a 'sno-ball', never a snow cone.
Finding the plastic baby in your king cake slice; whoever gets it buys the next cake.

designCues.cue: King cake sanding-sugar triad: purple #5B2C83, green #00843D and gold #F2B900 as glittering crystals over braided cinnamon-dough brown, not flat Carnival blocks.
designCues.source: The colored sugar on king cakes, in the Carnival colors Rex introduced in 1872.
designCues.use: Use a sugar-crystal speckle print or metallic-fleck knit for the January drop so it reads as cake rather than generic Mardi Gras.

designCues.cue: Nectar-cream pink #F5A3C7 with condensed-milk white #FFF8EC.
designCues.source: The pink nectar sno-ball at Hansen's and neighborhood stands.
designCues.use: A spring and summer colorway against Pelicans navy #0C2340 for shorts and sneaker accents that only locals will decode.

designCues.cue: Boiled-crawfish red #C2401F over a newspaper-covered boil table.
designCues.source: Backyard crawfish boils poured out onto newsprint from March to May.
designCues.use: Use it for late-season and play-in warmups with a newsprint-grain texture, and never reproduce real newspaper mastheads.

designCues.cue: Powdered sugar dusted over chicory-coffee brown (base #3B2A20).
designCues.source: Beignets and café au lait, the French Market breakfast every local has eaten.
designCues.use: A soft sugar-dust gradient on dark fleece, with no Café du Monde awning stripes or logos.

designCues.cue: Waxed white butcher-paper wrap with a hand-written 'dressed' order ticket.
designCues.source: How po-boy shops wrap and ticket every sandwich, and the 1929 streetcar-strike 'poor boy' origin.
designCues.use: Use it for packaging, hangtags and shoebox tissue, with the strike origin printed inside the box.

designCues.cue: Hand-painted lettering from corner-store, po-boy and sno-ball stand signs: chunky brush capitals, drop shadows, hand-ruled menu boards.
designCues.source: Neighborhood corner stores and seasonal stands across the city.
designCues.use: Commission New Orleans sign painters to letter collection names and wordmarks, and credit them on the tag.

designCues.cue: The tiny plastic king cake baby as a hidden detail.
designCues.source: The baby baked into every king cake, and the Pelicans' own King Cake Baby mascot.
designCues.use: Hide it inside a collar, under a tongue or on a waistband tab; the mascot is team-owned IP, so it is clear to use.

designCues.cue: Red-bean mosaic: dried beans set like beadwork to form images.
designCues.source: Krewe of Red Beans costumes for the Lundi Gras Red Beans Parade.
designCues.use: Commission and pay krewe bean artists for an original graphic, and don't imitate Black Masking Indian beadwork.

productHooks: Twelfth Night Pack (Jan 6, 2027): a sanding-sugar knit warmup and tee in purple, green and gold, with a hidden King Cake Baby on the waistband, sold in a king-cake-style box next to a paid, co-branded cake from a local bakery such as Dong Phuong.
'Dressed' Pelicans hoodie and tee shipped in waxed butcher paper with an order-ticket hangtag and the 1929 'poor boy' story inside, launched at the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

Nectar Cream colorway (pink #F5A3C7 on navy) for spring shorts, slides and, if his Jordan Brand signature line is still active, a Zion Williamson player-edition sneaker, launched with a paid sno-ball stand collab.
Red Beans Monday tee for Monday home games, designed with Krewe of Red Beans artists, with proceeds to Feed the Second Line.
Crawfish Season stretch-run pack: boiled-crawfish red warmups with a newsprint texture, timed to Lent and the Jazz Fest window.
Tết x Carnival capsule co-designed with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and launched at the Mary Queen of Vietnam festival weekend.
watchouts: Food brands are third-party IP. Café du Monde, Hubig's (Savory Simon), Zapp's (Utz), Barq's (Coca-Cola), Crystal (Baumer Foods), Camellia, Leidenheimer, Zatarain's (McCormick) and Kool-Aid (Kraft Heinz) all need licenses, so no lookalike trade dress. 'Red Beans and Ricely Yours' is tied to Louis Armstrong's legacy and needs clearance.

Second-line clubs, Black Masking Indian suits and the Holy Thursday table are Black community traditions. Don't lift club names, beadwork or vendors' identities; credit and pay culture bearers directly or through Feed the Second Line.
Voodoo is a living religion: skip voodoo-doll and 'Voodoo' chip gimmicks even though they're everywhere in the tourist food trade.
Partner conflicts: Smoothie King holds the arena naming rights and Gayle Benson owns Faubourg Brewing, so clear beverage categories with the team, and never revive Dixie Beer marks.

Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City face displacement, and the Claiborne overpass is still an open wound. Product that borrows their food without sending money back will be called out, and there should be no Katrina or Ida puns.

culture.headline: New Orleans sees itself as America's one true original that the rest of the country treats as a party or a problem, so its pride lives in wards, high schools and Black Creole street institutions that outlasted the levee failures and two departed basketball teams, not in a Pelicans brand that dates only to 2013.
culture.summary: New Orleans thinks of itself as the most original city in America: the place that made jazz, Creole cooking, Carnival and bounce, and the northernmost port of the Caribbean. It believes outsiders see a Bourbon Street party, a Katrina disaster story or a crime headline, and its chip on the shoulder is that it gave the country its culture and then had to rebuild itself after the federal levees failed in 2005. Pride is hyper-local (your ward, your high school, your club, your side of the river), and the deepest traditions, from Black Masking Indians and Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs to Baby Dolls and Leah Chase's gumbo z'herbes, come from Black and Creole-of-color New Orleanians in Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City. The Pelicans are a young brand in a Saints-first town whose fans watched the ABA Buccaneers and the Jazz leave and the Hornets spend two Katrina seasons in Oklahoma City, so loyalty is earned by showing up in neighborhoods. Nike's window is Twelfth Night through crawfish season, when the Saints are idle and the city's own calendar peaks.

insights.title: A party or a problem, says everyone else
insights.detail: Locals believe the country knows New Orleans through Bourbon Street, 'N'awlins' and 'the Big Easy', or through Katrina, crime and the Jan. 1, 2025 Bourbon Street truck attack. Their counter-story is authorship: Congo Square, jazz, Creole food, Carnival and bounce were made here, by them.
insights.implication: Write product voice in local terms ('Where y'at', 'Yeah you right', ward numbers) and lead with the city as creator. Beads-and-booze, voodoo caricature and disaster imagery read as tourist or outsider gear.

insights.title: The levees, not the storm
insights.detail: Katrina hit on Aug. 29, 2005, but locals stress that federal levee and floodwall failures put about 80% of the city under water, scattered families to Houston, Atlanta and Baton Rouge, and emptied neighborhoods like the Lower Ninth Ward. The Saints' Superdome return on Sept. 25, 2006 and the Super Bowl XLIV title in February 2010 became the civic resurrection, which is why the Saints still hold the city's emotional center.
insights.implication: Return-and-rebuild is the city's sacred text: tell it only in local voices, with restraint, and keep Aug. 29 for remembrance rather than product. The Pelicans' honest angle is 'still here', not borrowed resilience slogans.

insights.title: Basketball has left before
insights.detail: The ABA Buccaneers moved to Memphis in 1970, the Jazz (Pete Maravich's team) left for Salt Lake City in 1979 and kept the name, and the Hornets played most of 2005-07 in Oklahoma City, which then landed the Thunder. The NBA itself owned the team from 2010 to 2012 before Tom Benson bought it and renamed it the Pelicans in 2013, and worry about permanence surfaces in losing seasons like 2025-26's 26-56.
insights.implication: Fans reward permanence. Product that roots the team in place (ward, high school, river, state bird) and honors the city's own hoops lineage, from Maravich to the Chris Paul Hornets and the All-Star Games of 2008, 2014 and 2017, builds trust a logo alone cannot.

insights.title: Ward, school, side of the river
insights.detail: New Orleanians place each other with 'What school you went to?', meaning high school (St. Aug, Warren Easton, Edna Karr, McDonogh 35, Brother Martin, Jesuit, Newman), and by ward, which bounce records shout out by number (Third, Seventh, Ninth, Seventeenth). The West Bank (Algiers, Gretna, Marrero, Harvey), New Orleans East and 'Metry' each rep separately from the Eastbank core.
insights.implication: Build modular identity product: ward-numeral and high-school-coded pieces made with local artists and the schools (licensed and paid), so a fan wears their exact New Orleans instead of a generic city tee.

insights.title: Black and Creole institutions run the calendar
insights.detail: The city's defining traditions come from Black and Creole-of-color communities: Congo Square, Homer Plessy's 1892 test case organized by Seventh Ward Creoles, Ruby Bridges at William Frantz in 1960, the Claiborne Avenue oaks cut down for I-10, and the living institutions of Black Masking Indians, Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs, Baby Dolls and Skull & Bone gangs. Each has its own rules, hierarchy and calendar (Mardi Gras Day, St. Joseph's Night, Super Sunday, Sunday second lines).
insights.implication: Co-create and pay: commission chiefs, queens, club designers and Baby Doll groups, credit them by name, and time drops to their calendar. Never reproduce Indian suits, patches or chants on mass product.

insights.title: The pelican is a comeback story
insights.detail: The brown pelican is Louisiana's state bird, and the 'pelican in her piety' (a mother feeding her chicks from her own breast) has been on the state flag and seal since the 19th century. DDT wiped out Louisiana's pelicans by the early 1960s; birds reintroduced from Florida starting in 1968 recovered enough to come off the federal endangered list in 2009, a year before the BP spill put oiled pelicans on the news.
insights.implication: Give the team name a story locals can own: a self-sacrificing, back-from-zero bird that fits a rebuilding team. Use it on jock tags, liners and hangtags instead of the cartoon framing the 2013 rename was mocked for.

insights.title: Built for heat, costume and the Carnival-to-crawfish run
insights.detail: Summers are humid and stormy from May to September and hurricane season runs June 1 to Nov. 30, so the mild months (October to May) carry the festivals: Twelfth Night, Carnival, Super Sunday, French Quarter Fest, Jazz Fest and crawfish season. Locals keep costume closets, mask for Carnival and Halloween, and treat Sunday second lines as best-dressed occasions.
insights.implication: The NBA season is New Orleans' outdoor season, so design for 60-80°F parade days: light layers, seersucker and mesh, rain shells, and pieces built to be customized or costumed. Concentrate drops between Jan. 6 and the end of crawfish season, when the Pelicans have the city mostly to themselves.

places.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
places.why: Family-run since 1939 and the benchmark for the sno-ball, the city's hot-weather ritual of finely shaved ice and syrups like nectar cream.

people.name: Leah Chase
people.role: Chef of Dooky Chase's (1923-2019), the 'Queen of Creole Cuisine'

people.name: Ruby Bridges
people.role: Civil rights icon; founder of the Ruby Bridges Foundation
people.why: The city's most recognized living civil rights figure, tied to the Upper Ninth Ward; any school-integration story should go through her foundation.

people.name: Avery Johnson
people.role: St. Augustine High alum, 1999 NBA champion with the Spurs, former NBA and Alabama head coach

people.role: Point guard of the New Orleans Hornets, 2005-2011

people.name: Master P (Percy Miller)
people.role: No Limit Records founder from the Calliope projects (Third Ward)
people.why: A hoops-obsessed rap mogul (NBA preseason stints with Charlotte and Toronto) whose 'Bout it' and 'Ya heard me' spread New Orleans slang nationally; named UNO's president of basketball operations in 2023.

people.name: Gayle Benson
people.role: Owner of the Pelicans and the Saints

designCues.cue: Brown pelican chestnut (approx.), the dark rust of the bird's breeding-season neck, paired with its white head and yellow crown.
designCues.source: Louisiana's state bird, off the endangered list since 2009.
designCues.use: A nature-true tonal colorway (chestnut, bone white, crown yellow) for lifestyle product that tells the comeback story.

productHooks: 'What School You Went To?' pack: Pelicans tees, hoodies and shorts co-branded with New Orleans high school programs (St. Aug, Easton, Karr, McDonogh 35, Brother Martin and others) under school licenses, with proceeds and gear going to their teams.

'Ward Call' neighborhood collection: ward-numeral jerseys and tees drawn by an artist from each ward, plus the West Bank and New Orleans East, launched at ward-themed home nights between Twelfth Night and the All-Star break.
'Piety' story jacket: a navy warmup with an embroidered pelican-in-her-piety liner and a 'Union, Justice, Confidence' hangtag telling the brown pelican's comeback, for a rebuilding season.
'Boil Season' March-April drop: boil red, nectar pink and seersucker-panel shooting shirts and shorts for the stretch run and any Play-In push (Apr. 13-16, 2027), built for 80°F days.

'Comité' Black History Month capsule: Plessy's 1892 stand, Ruby Bridges' 1960 walk and Dooky Chase's back room, made with the Plessy & Ferguson Foundation and the Ruby Bridges Foundation, which approve the work and share the proceeds.
Second-line co-sign: pay a Social Aid & Pleasure Club to design a limited Pelicans sash, umbrella and shirt in its own colors, released after its parade so it never pre-empts the club's color reveal.
watchouts: Black Masking Indian suits, patches, songs and gang names are sacred, represent a year of handwork and belong to their makers: never print or imitate them, never use Native American headdress imagery, and use 'Black Masking Indians' or a gang's own name only with permission.

Katrina is grief, not a theme: no flood waterlines, search-and-rescue X-codes, blue tarps or Superdome-shelter imagery, nothing commercial on Aug. 29, and no party-on-Bourbon framing around the Jan. 1 anniversary of the 2025 attack.

Licensing: the Saints' fleur-de-lis rendering, 'Who Dat' (the NFL's 2010 cease-and-desist push against local tee makers caused a public backlash), krewe names, emblems and throws such as Zulu coconuts, high school marks, and Norman Rockwell's Ruby Bridges painting all need clearance.

Don't flatten the region: Cajun means Acadiana (Lafayette), not New Orleans Creole; locals don't say 'N'awlins' or 'the Big Easy'; and Louisiana Voodoo is a living religion, not a costume or skull graphic.
Use current place names: after the 2017 Confederate monument removals, Lee Circle became Harmony Circle and Jefferson Davis Parkway became Norman C. Francis Parkway.
