underground.headline: New Orleans taste is set on foot and in public: second-line suits matched to fresh sneakers, bounce and queer nightlife, and Black Mardi Gras culture that Nike should credit and never borrow.
underground.summary: The city's strongest subcultures are not skate or tuner scenes but living street traditions: Social Aid & Pleasure Club second lines, bounce music with its queer-led core, and the Mardi Gras Indian tradition. These scenes dress to be seen moving, so color-matched sneakers, custom suits, fans, sashes and hand-painted detail matter more than logos. Beneath them runs a smaller DIY and vintage layer along St. Claude Avenue, Magazine Street and the Bywater, plus a local-pride tee economy built on phrases rather than icons. The Pelicans are in a low-expectation season (26-56 last year, new coach Jamahl Mosley), so the credible play is neighborhood-first and culture-first, not a hype-driven team launch. Everything ceremonial is off limits; everything else needs local partners who are credited and paid.

insights.title: The second line is a sneaker runway
insights.detail: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as the Original Big 7, Black Men of Labor, Young Men Olympian Jr. and the Lady Buckjumpers parade most Sundays from fall to spring in custom suits, sashes, hats and fans, with shoes color-matched to each club's season outfit. Fresh Air Force 1s, Jordans and dress-casual sneakers are part of the look.
insights.implication: Offer clean, tonal sneaker colorways that can be matched to a club's colors, and approach clubs about a commissioned, credited colorway rather than putting a swoosh on their regalia.

insights.title: Bounce is the city's own sound, and its queer artists built it
insights.detail: Bounce grew out of the Magnolia and Calliope-era housing-project parties and was carried forward by Big Freedia, Katey Red, Sissy Nobby and DJ Jubilee. Its dance language (the shake, the buck) and its queer and trans center are what outsiders miss.
insights.implication: Build activations with bounce DJs and dancers on the stipend roster, treat the queer artists as lead voices, and design for movement: stretch, breathable and loose layers that survive a sweaty dance floor.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian craft is sacred, not a mood board
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian tribes sew new suits every year of beads, feathers and rhinestones, with Super Sunday and St. Joseph's night as the key gatherings. The Backstreet Cultural Museum in Tremé is the community-run archive of this tradition.
insights.implication: Do not reproduce suit imagery, patches or tribe iconography on product. If Nike engages at all, it is through the Backstreet Museum and tribal members on their own terms, with payment and veto power.

insights.title: The tee economy runs on phrases, not logos
insights.detail: Local brands like Dirty Coast turned neighborhood talk and in-jokes into the city's best-selling tees, and locals wear them over team gear. People signal belonging by the specificity of the reference.
insights.implication: Use ward, neighborhood and phrase typography on City Edition-adjacent tees, and consider a collaboration with a local brand instead of an outside agency voice.

insights.title: St. Claude and the Bywater hold the DIY layer
insights.detail: Zeitgeist Multi-Disciplinary Arts Center, the AllWays Lounge and the Hi-Ho Lounge anchor the experimental, zine, drag and punk crowd along St. Claude Avenue and in the Marigny. Vintage and thrift buyers shop Magazine Street and the Bywater, remixing old Saints, Hornets and Pelicans jerseys with local tees.
insights.implication: Source heritage Hornets teal-and-purple and early Pelicans looks for a vintage-inspired capsule, and seed the pieces through these venues and local thrift buyers rather than mall retail.

insights.title: Zion fandom is loyal but frustrated
insights.detail: A second straight sub-30-win season, a quiet offseason and a new coach leave local fans loyal to the city and the club but less convinced about the roster. Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears are the younger names the street-level crowd can adopt.
insights.implication: Lead with city identity and rising players, not a championship narrative. Keep the team tie light and let neighborhoods carry the story.

hoops.headline: New Orleans hoops lives in neighborhood gyms, Catholic League and public-school rivalries, and second-line rhythm, and the Pelicans are claimed more through the city than the other way round.
hoops.summary: Basketball in New Orleans is a neighborhood and school-pride culture first: Edna Karr, St. Augustine, Warren Easton, McDonogh 35, Landry-Walker, John Curtis and Holy Cross carry more block-level loyalty than any pro franchise. The Pelicans entered 2026-27 coming off 26-56, a second straight sub-30-win year, with first-year coach Jamahl Mosley, Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears and low expectations. That makes local identity, not winning, the activation currency: the 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' purple-and-neon-green 'Skelican' City Edition was a fan favorite and was brought back in 2025-26. Locals dress for heat and humidity, with mesh, long shorts, school and neighborhood tees, and the Saints and Mardi Gras palette bleeding into everything. Nike's way in is through gyms, school programs and Black-led cultural institutions, with credit and payment, not a fleur-de-lis stamped on a jersey.

insights.title: School colors outrank the NBA team
insights.detail: Programs like St. Augustine (Purple Knights), Edna Karr, Warren Easton, McDonogh 35, Landry-Walker and John Curtis carry multi-generational loyalty, and a Friday-night or district-rivalry game is a bigger local event than a mid-week Pelicans game in a losing season.
insights.implication: Build school-level and neighborhood-level collections and team-sale programs, not just Pelicans merch; a purple-and-gold or maroon school-pride capsule reads as local in a way an NBA logo does not.

insights.title: Rebuilding team, lowered fan temperature
insights.detail: Two straight sub-30-win seasons, a coaching change (Willie Green out, Jamahl Mosley in), no 2026 first-round pick and a quiet summer under Joe Dumars mean fans are fatigued, though Zion Williamson and Trey Murphy III still draw attention.
insights.implication: Lead with the city and its hoopers, not the standings; product that celebrates New Orleans identity holds value when the team is not winning.

insights.title: Heat and humidity dictate the on-court look
insights.detail: Summer and early-fall runs happen in extreme humidity, in open-air or poorly cooled neighborhood gyms, so hoopers favor breathable mesh, sleeveless or short-sleeve tops and layered tees for the walk to the court.
insights.implication: Prioritize ultra-light mesh and moisture-wicking Dri-FIT pieces plus shorter-sleeve shooting shirts; cold-weather hoops product matters less here than in Portland.

insights.title: Second-line and Mardi Gras energy is the city's visual grammar
insights.detail: Neighborhood social aid and pleasure clubs, brass bands and Mardi Gras parades set a color and movement vocabulary of purple, green, gold, sequins and fringe that locals recognize instantly.
insights.implication: Use the palette and rhythm of celebration on City Edition and lifestyle pieces, but keep sacred Black Masking Indian suiting imagery off product unless a Black Masking Indian partner leads and is paid.

insights.title: Local pro basketball beyond the Pelicans is thin

fanbase.headline: Pelicans fans are a small, fiercely local, Saints-first and Mardi Gras-literate base who love the city's culture louder than the team's results, and are tired of waiting for a Zion-led payoff.
fanbase.summary: New Orleans is a Saints, LSU and Mardi Gras town first, and the Pelicans hold a loyal but modest slice of it, strongest among diehards who stayed through the Hornets-to-Pelicans transition and the Anthony Davis years. Two straight sub-30-win seasons (26-56 last year), a quiet offseason under Joe Dumars, and a new coach in Jamahl Mosley have left the mood weary and wait-and-see rather than angry. Zion Williamson is still the emotional lightning rod, Trey Murphy III is the player fans actually trust, and second-year players Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears supply the hope. The fan wears the city, not just the team: fleur-de-lis, Mardi Gras purple-green-gold, and local brands sit beside navy and gold Pelicans gear, and the best City Edition moments have come when the team leaned into that.

insights.title: Saints-first town, Pels as the second love
insights.detail: Football, LSU and Carnival dominate the calendar and the closet in New Orleans, so Pelicans gear competes with black-and-gold Saints and purple-and-gold LSU apparel for the same wardrobe slot. Pelicans passion is real but concentrated, and it peaks when the team tells a New Orleans story instead of a generic NBA one.
insights.implication: Lead Pelicans product with city iconography (fleur-de-lis, Carnival, second-line) rather than team marks alone, and avoid directly mimicking Saints black and gold.

insights.title: Fatigue, not fury, is the mood
insights.detail: Last season finished 26-56 and missed the playoffs for the second straight sub-30-win year. Fans are watching a coach change from Willie Green to Jamahl Mosley, no 2026 first-round pick (traded to Atlanta in the Derik Queen deal), and a quiet summer.
insights.implication: Keep early-season product and campaigns about the city and the young core, not championship promises. Trey Murphy III, Queen and Fears are safer faces than anything built on Zion availability.

insights.title: Zion is the brand, Murphy is the trust
insights.detail: Zion Williamson draws national attention and the biggest jersey and sneaker interest, but years of injury interruptions made fans cautious about hanging identity on him. Trey Murphy III, who averaged 21.5 ppg and survived June trade rumors, is the locally admired homegrown-feeling scorer.
insights.implication: Balance Zion signature storytelling with Murphy and young-core product so a single availability story does not govern the line. Zion is already a Jordan Brand athlete, so coordinate any Jordan crossover thinking.

insights.title: Hornets-era memory is the elder's tattoo
insights.detail: Older fans remember the 2002-2013 Hornets era and the Chris Paul, David West, Tyson Chandler and Byron Scott years, plus the 2005-07 Oklahoma City exile after Katrina. Teal and purple Hornets throwbacks still circulate in the city, and the name Pelicans arrived in 2013.
insights.implication: A Hornets-era-adjacent teal and purple heritage gesture could resonate, but the Hornets name and marks belong to Charlotte, so any use needs clear licensing and care.

insights.title: City Edition is the fan's favorite product moment
insights.detail: Per the current facts, the 2025-26 City Edition resurrected the 2023-24 fan-favorite design, which signals that the audience rewards local storytelling and punishes generic. The 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' edition (purple and neon green, a skeletal 'Skelican') shows fans reward a nocturnal, local-feeling look over generic team color.
insights.implication: Treat the City Edition as the anchor drop for the market and pair it with a lifestyle capsule rooted in Carnival color blocking, built with local collaborators.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian imagery is not a motif to lift
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits and the Tremé and Seventh Ward second-line brass-band culture are sacred community traditions made by the maskers over a full year. Fans love and display the culture but the community is protective of it.
insights.implication: Any reference needs Black New Orleans partners credited and paid, and the suits themselves should not be reproduced as a pattern. Safer cues are the bold, unaffiliated visual languages of Carnival parades, social aid and pleasure club umbrella and sash color play, and brass-band typography.

rhythm.headline: New Orleans watches the Pelicans in the gaps between its own calendar: Saints Sundays, LSU Saturdays, and a Carnival season that swallows February whole.
rhythm.summary: The Pelicans fan year is a low-expectations, high-loyalty rhythm: 26-56 last season, a new coach in Jamahl Mosley, no 2026 first-round pick, and no opening-night or Christmas national showcase. Engagement peaks in late October through December when the Saints and LSU are not yet the only story, then gets pushed aside by Carnival in January and February and by Jazz Fest, crawfish season and hurricane season later. Fans here buy culture first and team second, so the highest-leverage retail moments are the ones where basketball touches Mardi Gras, second-line season, Essence weekend and Zion or Trey Murphy III moments rather than standings. The city's own calendar, not the NBA's, tells you when a Pelicans product feels native.

insights.title: Carnival is the real February
insights.detail: Carnival season starts January 6 and Mardi Gras Day is February 9, 2027, so the stretch between the trade deadline (Feb 11) and All-Star weekend (Feb 19-21) lands right on the post-Carnival hangover. Parade routes, school closures and the krewe calendar dominate attention; Pelicans games compete with Endymion, Bacchus and Zulu weekends.
insights.implication: Do not launch a Pelicans hero drop in the two weeks before Mardi Gras. Instead, make Carnival-adjacent product (purple, green and gold throwback energy, throw-style graphics) a January pre-sale that can bridge to the team.

insights.title: Saints and LSU own fall and winter Sundays and Saturdays
insights.detail: Saints games and LSU football in Baton Rouge fill September through early January, so the Pelicans opener (league tips off Oct 20; their own date to confirm) and November Cup nights compete with football. Casual fans tune in more after the Saints season ends in January.
insights.implication: Time Pelicans apparel drops to Friday Cup nights and weekday evenings, and use cross-fandom co-branding (Gulf South pride, not Saints marks) rather than fighting Sunday; the Saints and Pelicans share an owner, so any joint story needs a licensing and relationship check.

insights.title: Cup group play is the early-season hook
insights.detail: The Pelicans are in NBA Cup West Group B with OKC, Minnesota, the Clippers and Memphis, opening Oct 30 at the Clippers. The Memphis game is the nearest regional rivalry on the schedule, and Cup games land on Fridays.
insights.implication: Use Cup nights for a limited Cup-colorway or Friday-night capsule; a Memphis matchup is the natural Gulf South and Mississippi River storyline for a regional graphic.

insights.title: Hope is player-driven, not result-driven
insights.detail: Two straight sub-30-win seasons mean the fan base attaches to individuals: Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III (who survived June trade rumors), and second-year players Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears. A new coach adds a fresh-start story in October.
insights.implication: Lead with player-driven product (Murphy and Zion signature or player-edition apparel, Queen and Fears youth sizing) rather than team-success playoff gear, which should be treated as an upside scenario only.

insights.title: Spring is for the city, not the standings
insights.detail: If the team misses the playoffs again, April and May belong to Jazz Fest (late April to early May), crawfish boils and festival season, with the Pelicans nearly invisible; the draft lottery and a possible high pick restores some engagement.
insights.implication: Plan April and May as a non-basketball brand-in-the-city window: festival-ready lightweight apparel and Nike Basketball showing up in neighborhood courts and brass band culture, not Pelicans performance gear.

insights.title: Summer is weather-locked and tourist-heavy
insights.detail: June to September is heat, afternoon storms and hurricane season, and Essence Festival around July 4 brings a huge influx of Black visitors and national culture to the Superdome and Smoothie King Center area; Southern Decadence at Labor Day draws another tourist wave.
insights.implication: Essence weekend is the best summer retail and storytelling moment for a Black-owned-creator collaboration; Pelicans product sold to visitors needs to read as New Orleans, not generic NBA.

uniform.headline: The Pelicans have a young identity, navy and gold with a fleur-de-lis pelican, and a fanbase that wants the city's real second-line and Mardi Gras Indian color on the jersey instead of a tourist-guide version.
uniform.summary: The Pelicans launched in 2013 with a navy, gold and red palette and a pelican-with-fleur-de-lis mark, replacing the Hornets' teal and purple, which stayed with Charlotte. The 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' City Edition (purple with neon green and a skeletal 'Skelican' mark, a night-streets concept rather than a Mardi Gras one) was loved enough that the 2025-26 City Edition brought it back. The brand has no deep classic era of its own, so New Orleans-made merch (Saints-adjacent Who Dat culture, second-line style, local screen-printers) fills the gap. The opening is real local storytelling, built with the people who own those traditions, on a team entering 2026-27 with low expectations, a new coach (Jamahl Mosley) and a 26-56 season behind it.

insights.title: Young identity, no deep classic era
insights.detail: The Pelicans brand dates to 2013 and the franchise's 2002-13 Hornets history sits with Charlotte, so there is no multi-decade throwback vault to mine. Fans' emotional anchors are Anthony Davis, Chris Paul-era Hornets memories, and Zion.
insights.implication: Classic Edition is a weak lever here. Nike should put its design energy into City Edition and lifestyle product built from the city, not the franchise archive.

insights.title: A returning City Edition shows what fans want
insights.detail: The 2025-26 City Edition reissued the 2023-24 design, which fans had singled out as a favorite. A team repeating a City Edition signals unusually strong demand for one look.
insights.implication: Study what made the 2023-24 design land before briefing a 2026-27 concept, and avoid replacing it with something more generic. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition status first.

insights.title: Mardi Gras purple, green and gold is expected but flattened
insights.detail: Carnival purple, green and gold is the city's default shorthand (the 2023-24 'Skelican' edition used purple and neon green but as a night-life look). Locals read Carnival color as a given, so fans respond more to specifics: krewe culture, the Zulu and Rex traditions, and the neighborhood second-line clubs.
insights.implication: Move from the generic three-color stripe to named, credited local references, with purple, green and gold used with restraint against navy.

insights.title: Real merch lives in New Orleans culture, not team shops
insights.detail: Local screen-printed shirts, Who Dat-style vernacular, Saints and Pelicans crossovers and neighborhood-pride tees (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, Westbank, Uptown) move more than generic team gear. Fans trade on area codes, wards and slang.
insights.implication: Collaborate with local New Orleans printers and designers, and build neighborhood-first graphics that the team's own shop does not.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian and second-line craft is the biggest untouched design language
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits, hand-sewn beadwork and feather work, and brass-band second-line parades from the Tremé and Seventh Ward are the city's most distinctive visual tradition. They are sacred and living, not decoration.
insights.implication: Treat this as a partnership, credit and pay the tribes' and artists' communities, and borrow the logic (color layering, patchwork, hand-stitched texture) rather than lifting suit imagery.

insights.title: Zion and Murphy are the faces, but the team is rebuilding fan trust
insights.detail: After two sub-30-win seasons, a 26-56 record and a coaching change to Jamahl Mosley, fan sentiment is cautious. Zion Williamson remains the marquee jersey, with Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears as the younger faces.
insights.implication: Lean on player product (Zion, Murphy) and on city pride rather than team-performance narratives, and keep launch volume measured.

retail-landscape.headline: New Orleans buys its taste locally and its volume in the suburbs: Magazine Street and homegrown fleur-de-lis brands set the look, while Metairie malls, Dillard's and Dick's move the units.
retail-landscape.summary: Basketball retail here is thin next to football and Mardi Gras. The Saints and local city-pride brands own the Gulf South gear wallet, and the Pelicans sit below them. Taste lives in a few uptown and Bywater shops plus pop-ups at second lines, festivals and Black-owned culture spaces. Volume lives in Metairie, Gretna and Kenner, and online. A Nike door strategy here is mostly about winning city-pride credibility, not adding square footage. After back-to-back sub-30-win seasons and a new coach in Jamahl Mosley, Zion and Trey Murphy III are the only real Pelicans retail pulls.

insights.title: The Saints wallet and city-pride brands outsell the Pelicans
insights.detail: Fleur-de-lis, 'Who Dat' and NOLA-pride tees from local brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl are what locals wear daily. Pelicans gear competes for the same shirt-drawer slot, and Pelicans fans often wear city-first rather than team-first.
insights.implication: Lead Pelicans and City Edition product with New Orleans iconography first and the team mark second, so it passes as city pride rather than team merch.

insights.title: Taste is set on Magazine Street and in the Bywater and Marigny, volume in Jefferson Parish
insights.detail: Uptown Magazine Street holds the independent boutiques and vintage; the Lakeside, Riverwalk and West Bank (Oakwood) malls hold the athletic chains and department stores where families buy sneakers and jerseys.
insights.implication: Seed limited drops and collabs in tastemaker doors and local pop-ups, then flow mainstream colorways to Foot Locker, Dick's and Dillard's in the suburbs.

insights.title: Real sneaker culture is community-run, not boutique-led
insights.detail: New Orleans has fewer destination sneaker boutiques than Atlanta or Houston. Sneaker and hoops culture runs through school and AAU hoops, park courts, resale meetups and Black-owned apparel brands, and much of it sells through social media and pop-ups.
insights.implication: Fund activations with local creators and pop-up hosts rather than a single flagship, and treat Instagram-driven local sellers as the retail scene.

insights.title: The arena team store is a game-night door, not a destination
insights.detail: The Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center and the arena's pop-up kiosks capture event-night buyers, and the season-ticket base is modest after two losing seasons. Fanatics and the team's online store carry the rest of the team-gear volume.
insights.implication: Use the arena store for City Edition launch moments, Zion and Trey Murphy III player-tee drops, and Cup-night giveaways, and keep inventory depth online.

insights.title: Tourists distort the French Quarter and Canal Street picture
insights.detail: Canal Place, Riverwalk and the Quarter's souvenir shops see huge traffic, but it is visitor spend on Saints, Mardi Gras and generic NOLA gear, not local basketball demand.
insights.implication: Treat tourist districts as brand-visibility and Mardi Gras-season merchandising spots, not as read-throughs for local Pelicans demand.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian and second-line imagery is a licensing and respect line
insights.detail: Suits, feathers and beadwork belong to specific Black neighborhood tribes and the social aid and pleasure clubs, and the community is protective of how they are used. Commercial lifting without credit has drawn criticism.
insights.implication: Work only through paid collaboration with named artists and clubs, and keep product abstracted from ceremonial imagery.

retail-behavior.headline: New Orleans shops on a Carnival-and-festival calendar, not a school calendar: spend spikes around Mardi Gras, Essence, Bayou Classic and Sunday second lines, and the Pelicans are a value-minded, Saints- and LSU-shadowed purchase.
retail-behavior.summary: This is a high-tourism, moderate-income, culture-first market where a fan's wardrobe is built for events (parades, second lines, tailgates, festivals) more than for a basketball schedule. Hot, humid weather for most of the year means short sleeves, shorts and lightweight fabrics dominate, with only a few real cold weeks. The Pelicans come off 26-56 and a second straight sub-30-win season under first-year coach Jamahl Mosley, so team-gear demand is driven by Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and the City Edition rather than by winning. Local purchasing is price-conscious and swingman-heavy, while the visitor stream (convention, Carnival, festival and Bayou Classic crowds) pays more and buys city-specific souvenirs. The sharpest commercial play is to tie drops to Louisiana's own calendar and to sell New Orleans itself, not just the team.

insights.title: Carnival is the real Q1 retail peak
insights.detail: Carnival season runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day, which falls on Feb 9 in 2027, and locals buy purple, green and gold gear, throw-related items and parade-day outfits in the weeks before. The Pelicans' home calendar competes with parade routes, and many fans plan around krewe schedules.
insights.implication: Time a Carnival-adjacent capsule for mid-January availability, not February, and keep it about the city's wardrobe (hoodies, tees, caps) rather than literal throws or krewe marks.

insights.title: Weather says light layers, with a short real winter
insights.detail: Summers are hot and humid and hurricane season runs June to November; genuine cold is a few weeks from December to February, and rain is frequent year-round. Fans buy shorts and breathable tees far longer than northern markets, and buy a hoodie or light jacket for the cold snaps and for over-air-conditioned arenas.
insights.implication: Weight assortments toward lightweight tees, shorts, quarter-zips and water-resistant shells; outerwear should be thin, packable and rain-ready, not heavy puffer.

insights.title: Festival and heritage events outrank the NBA calendar for spend
insights.detail: Essence Festival of Culture over July 4th weekend, Jazz Fest in late April and early May, the Bayou Classic over Thanksgiving weekend (Grambling vs Southern in the Superdome), and Southern Decadence on Labor Day weekend each pull in large shopper crowds that overlap with the NBA offseason or fall start. Essence in particular brings a national Black audience with real spending power.
insights.implication: Plan pop-ups and city-product drops around Essence and Bayou Classic, which reach both locals and out-of-town buyers when the Pelicans are not playing, and partner with HBCU and Black-owned local voices.

insights.title: Sunday second lines are the local social-commerce engine
insights.detail: Social aid and pleasure clubs parade most Sundays from roughly September to May in custom-dyed matching outfits, and the outfits, suits, fans and sneakers are commissioned and photographed heavily on Instagram. Mardi Gras Indian culture runs a parallel, deeply craft-based season, with Super Sunday in March and St. Joseph's night around March 19.
insights.implication: Treat second-line fashion as a custom, color-matched, sneaker-forward market: offer color-coordinated team colorways and customization, and engage clubs as paid collaborators rather than using imagery.

insights.title: Price-sensitive locals, higher-spending visitors
insights.detail: Orleans Parish has a large lower-income population alongside a hospitality workforce paid in tips, so cash flow follows tourist seasons, tax-refund season and Carnival work. Visitors, by contrast, buy a premium souvenir piece and often a jersey on a trip.
insights.implication: Tier the range: accessible swingman, kids and tees for local households, plus a premium city-keepsake tier and authentic pieces aimed at visitors and out-of-state Pelicans fans.

insights.title: The Pelicans compete with Saints, LSU and Tulane for the wallet
insights.detail: Football season (Saints, LSU in Baton Rouge, Tulane) and the Sugar Bowl on New Year's Day set the fall and winter fan calendar, and Pelicans gear is often the second or third team purchase. Team sentiment is cool after back-to-back sub-30-win seasons and a quiet offseason with no 2026 first-round pick.
insights.implication: Lead with Zion, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears and with the City Edition rather than the standings; use Cup nights and a new-coach narrative for early-season hooks.

extra.priceProfile: Orleans Parish is lower-income with a high poverty rate alongside an affluent Uptown and Garden District, and household cash flow is tied to tips and seasonal hospitality work. Locals respond to accessible price points, bundles and kids' value tiers, while visitors will pay for a premium or limited city-specific piece. Louisiana's combined state and Orleans local sales tax is roughly 10 percent as of 2025 and there is no standing back-to-school tax holiday, so price tags should be read as all-in at checkout.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Local fans lean toward swingman jerseys and tees at lower price points, with kids' jerseys the major gifting item, while authentic jerseys are bought mostly by committed fans and visitors. Zion Williamson is the leading name, with Trey Murphy III rising, and the City Edition is the key limited moment. Knockoffs and unlicensed festival-vendor shirts are part of the local streetwear economy and set the price anchor for official product.

factcheck.summary: The dossiers are largely accurate on the Pelicans' 2026-27 facts, Cup schedule and Carnival-calendar dates, but a live check found the central City Edition premise wrong: the 2023-24 design brought back in 2025-26 is the purple-and-neon-green 'NOLA Nights' Skelican edition, not a Mardi Gras one, so five dossiers were fixed and the brief's 'Carnival palette is spent' rationale is flagged for the editor. Smaller fixes covered rookie status for Queen and Fears, Xavier and Mardi Gras World locations, Fleurty Girl's doors and founder name, and several oddly specific music, food and art details. The remaining queue lists business, venue and schedule claims that need a live check, plus brief issues around unknown home dates and the Nov 27 Bayou Classic and Black Friday overlap.

issues.problem: The brief treats Corner Tile as if it could reach the court soon, but the 2026-27 City Edition is already designed, approved and in production, and the brief never says it is a 2027-28 concept. Nothing in the calendar sets the NBA approval window for the next set, and the Association set is already white-based.
issues.fix: Label Corner Tile as the 2027-28 City Edition pitch with a back-planned approval timeline. For 2026-27, run the tile, iron-lace and ward language on lifestyle product that rides the existing City Edition. Pull Glazed White as the base or define it clearly against the Association white, since NBA rules require the two sets to contrast.

issues.problem: Ward Call is launched at a 'home opener' whose date is unverified (the Oct 20 opening-night slate does not include New Orleans, and the first known Pelicans game is Oct 30 at the Clippers). The pack also needs one paid artist per ward, many school licenses, high-school sign-offs and a Big Freedia booking within about three weeks.
issues.fix: Phase it. Launch with two or three wards and a handful of schools at the first confirmed home game, and put the full 17 wards and the school co-brands on a Dec to Feb rollout. Hold the Freedia set until her footwear and apparel status is cleared, and lead with a bounce lineup with named queer pioneers (Katey Red, Sissy Nobby).

issues.problem: Licensed co-brands with St. Aug, Edna Karr, Warren Easton and McDonogh 35 involve minors, school marks and athletic departments that may be tied to other brands, plus LHSAA and Orleans Parish and charter-network rules. The brief calls this licensing but names no process.
issues.fix: Start with one willing program or alumni association, route everything through the school's licensing and athletic office, and make the giveback (gear, gym or team funds) the headline. Treat the school line as a 2027 phase-two item, not an October launch item.

issues.problem: The Bayou Classic band collaboration is built around St. Augustine's Marching 100 (a New Orleans high school band), but the Battle of the Bands is between Southern and Grambling. The drop also lands on Nov 27, which is a Cup Friday, with the Superdome area full of rival-brand HBCU tailgates.
issues.fix: Either center the Bayou Classic piece on HBCU-coded product with the two universities' own licensing and band programs (and Xavier and Dillard locally), or keep the St. Aug collaboration as a separate local brass story outside Classic weekend. Check the Pelicans' Nov 27 schedule before planning a pop-up.

issues.problem: One headline artist is carrying the whole bounce story. Bounce credit sits with a group (Katey Red, Sissy Nobby, DJ Jubilee and others) and a single paid booking risks reading as star-casting, while her footwear and apparel obligations are unknown.
issues.fix: Pay a rotating roster of bounce artists and DJs for the ward call-and-response, put the credit on the product and in the arena, and offer the commission to bounce pioneers before the headliner.

issues.target: partners[Dirty Coast, Fleurty Girl] rapid-response tees
issues.problem: The plan has local brands make quick player tees, but player names and numbers sit under NBA and NBPA group licensing, which a local brand cannot sublicense, and the brief itself notes the 'Who Dat' history. A pre-cleared program is not feasible on a days-long turnaround without those approvals.
issues.fix: Make the rapid-response tees city-only (no player likenesses), or get Pelicans and NBPA clearance up front for a fixed list of designs and a fixed turn time. Keep the local brands as co-designers of the voice, and pay them as such.

issues.problem: The Twelfth Night Pack leans on purple, green and gold at the same time as the brief says the Carnival palette is spent and the fan-favorite City Edition already owns it. The King Cake Baby hunt and co-branded cake are fun but thin as a design idea, and the food co-brand has shipping, shelf-life and food-safety limits.
issues.fix: Keep the sanding-sugar texture and the Baby, but cut the palette to a navy ground with a small fleck, and run the cake as an in-arena giveaway rather than a bundled retail item. Confirm Pelicans ownership of the King Cake Baby for apparel before building around it.

issues.problem: A Tết x Carnival tee is tied to a church-centered family holiday that has just been commercially adjacent to Carnival, with a short window before Mardi Gras Day. Pairing a community's New Year with a Carnival theme risks making it a novelty, and the brief names the Mary Queen of Vietnam gathering in a drop plan.
issues.fix: Move it off the product calendar. Instead fund or host a community moment (Vietnamese New Orleanian artists paid to design a Pelicans game-night element, or Dong Phuong as a named food partner), and ask the community whether a product is wanted at all.

issues.problem: The plan assumes 'Cup Friday home nights', a Memphis rivalry graphic and a Cup-colorway capsule, but only the Oct 30 Cup opener (at the Clippers) is known and the home dates are unconfirmed. There is also no Cup-specific uniform, only the standard sets, so a Cup colorway is not a product the brief can promise.
issues.fix: Tie Cup activations to confirmed home dates only, and use a generic Friday-night-in-New-Orleans graphic that works for any Cup opponent. Drop the 'Cup colorway' language. Keep the Memphis graphic only if the home date is confirmed.

issues.target: calendar (Oak Street Po-Boy Festival, Red Beans Monday tee)
issues.problem: A hoodie wrapped in butcher paper and a Monday red-beans tee are novelty food references with no clear fan, price or reason to buy, and a November hoodie for a festival that is only a day of walking. They read like tourist-guide gags beside the stronger craft ideas.
issues.fix: Fold them into one community gesture, such as paying Feed the Second Line and the Krewe of Red Beans to design a Monday home-night element, and cut the Po-Boy Festival item.

issues.problem: The club commission is the best idea in the brief but the plan has Nike underwriting parade permits and police fees, pushing a release 'the week after the parade' and calling it a limited sneaker, while club colors stay secret until parade day. A release that depends on a club's schedule, cannot be previewed and needs its sign-off conflicts with Nike's lead times and could be read as buying the culture.
issues.fix: Make the first season a no-product pilot: pay the club and band, fund fees through a culture-bearer intermediary, and let the club decide whether and when product exists. Plan a numbered, small-run, club-owned release only if the club asks for one.

issues.problem: The brief gives the museum 'veto rights' as an introducer and advisor, but the museum is a small community institution, not a gatekeeper for every club or tribe, and the clubs and tribes must consent for themselves.
issues.fix: Treat the museum as one paid advisor, ask it who else should be at the table, and get written consent from each club and band directly. Keep the Black Masking Indian line as 'no product, no reference' and do not use Super Sunday or St. Joseph's Night in any plan.

issues.problem: The Claiborne Oaks story turns a documented loss to a Black neighborhood (the overpass that removed the oaks) into a product theme. It is credible only if the artists lead, and putting it on an NBA uniform as an alternate puts a community wound under a swoosh.
issues.fix: Keep it as an artist-owned capsule with the artists choosing the beneficiary and the credit, and take it off the uniform alternates list. Brief it to Studio BE only as an invitation, with the ability to decline.

issues.target: topInsights and collection (fleur-de-lis and Code Noir)
issues.problem: The Code Noir fleur-de-lis point is stated as settled fact in the avoid list. The historical use of the mark in branding is real but contested in how it is told, and the Pelicans' own mark already uses the fleur-de-lis, so the brief's stance conflicts with the team's identity.
issues.fix: Say plainly that the fleur-de-lis is avoided mainly because it reads as Saints and as tourist shorthand, mention the history as a secondary reason, and note the Pelicans mark itself already carries it.

issues.problem: Lent starts Feb 10, so fish fries and crawfish boil season begin just after Mardi Gras, not 'mid-March'. Boil Season is also tied to a Play-In push that a 26-56 team may not have, and it overlaps with Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night in the same weeks.
issues.fix: Start the Boil Season story in late February or early March around the team's actual schedule, keep the Play-In tee as a contingency only, and avoid Super Sunday weekend (Mar 14, 2027) and St. Joseph's Night (Mar 19) entirely.

issues.problem: The hoops and retail dossiers point to Xavier, Dillard, Southern and the HBCU fan base, LHSAA playoffs (when school pride peaks, Feb to March), the Sugar Bowl crowd, and Louisiana-wide Gulf South fans (Baton Rouge, Acadiana, the Gulf Coast). The brief uses none of these as a partner or window.
issues.fix: Add an HBCU capsule with Xavier and Dillard (and Southern and Grambling for Classic), a Friday-night school-rivalry home night timed to the LHSAA playoffs, and a Gulf South regional product line sold outside the metro.

issues.problem: The underground dossier's St. Claude and Marigny layer (Zeitgeist, AllWays Lounge, Hi-Ho), drag and Southern Decadence are barely used, and the actual courts (Joe W. Brown Park, Behrman) and summer heat-led hooper needs appear only as a heat note in the retail playbook.
issues.fix: Make one court-based activation at Joe W. Brown or Behrman with mesh and sleeveless product, and a Southern Decadence or Halloween bounce night with the queer artists credited. Both are pitched as paid collaborations, not drops.

issues.target: pulse and risks (Zion and Jordan Brand)
issues.problem: Zion is flagged as a Jordan Brand conflict, but the brief still assigns him 'kids swingman' and player tees in the holiday core and lists the Murphy-first strategy without checking Nike's own relationships with Murphy, Queen and Fears. Player product also depends on which of them Nike actually signs.
issues.fix: Confirm each player's apparel arrangement before assigning product, run Zion pieces through Jordan Brand, and make the Nike-signed names the lead in the holiday plan. Without that, lead with city and ward product in the holiday window.

issues.problem: The brief says 'sell the city, not the team' for a team whose product it also needs to move. The 56 opportunity score looks high given retail 34 and fandom 38, and the plan sets a 70% sell-through KPI by Feb 1 for a regional market with a small team-gear base.
issues.fix: Lower the sell-through target, set an expectation per tier (entry tees versus premium), and say how much of the plan is team-branded. Consider an opportunity score nearer the mid-40s.

strengths: The strategy puts the city mark first and the team mark second, and it grounds that in real local behavior: phrase tees over team gear, ward and school identity, and the Saints and LSU competing for the same closet.

The Corner Tile concept (tile street names, iron-lace, sign-painter lettering, brass) passes the swap test, avoids the Carnival palette the fan-favorite City Edition already owns, and keeps Black Masking Indian beadwork and ceremonial imagery out.

The calendar follows the city's own clock (king cake, Mardi Gras Day on Feb 9, 2027, second-line season, Essence, Jazz Fest) and sensibly keeps hero launches out of the two weeks before Carnival and away from Super Sunday and Aug 29.
The pay-and-credit stance is specific: parade fees, instruments through named programs, proceeds to community groups chosen by the artists, and credit on the product.
Weighting the plan toward city-first product that can sell regardless of the standings is the right call for a 26-56 team with a new coach and a thin retail base.
critique.summary: Strong on culture and specificity, with a genuinely un-swappable design language and a careful line on sacred material, but weaker on delivery. The biggest problems are feasibility and timing: Corner Tile cannot be the 2026-27 uniform, Ward Call and its school licensing are overloaded for an October launch with an unverified home opener, NBA and NBPA licensing blocks the rapid-response tee idea, and the Bayou Classic band plan mixes up which bands are involved. The brief also skips HBCU, LHSAA and Gulf South opportunities in its own dossiers. Fix the sequencing, phase the community partnerships so the communities set the terms, and cut the novelty items, and it holds up.
